$comment: THE LOOP'S OWN EVIDENCE. Every run here was executed against the runtimes deployed on Ethereum
mainnet: the images were strings returned by eth_call to IArtRuntimeV1.renderV1, they were
rasterised, and a reviewer that was not the author looked at them and wrote the verdict recorded
NO IMAGES ARE STORED. Hashes and paths, because a record with pictures inside it is a record
nobody opens. The render commitment is sha256 over sorted `<name> <sha256(bytes)>` lines, the
same algorithm the template catalog publishes, so a reader with the chain can recompute it.
A REFUSAL IS A RESULT. Runs that ended ART_QUALITY_NOT_ACCEPTABLE are kept, not deleted: a loop
that has never refused anything has not been shown to be able to.

critique.observation: Nothing in this packet is a cairn. The brief asks for one stacked stone marker with a top and a bottom, made of a few large rough courses, standing alone in an empty field. What renders is a single flat axis-aligned square or a single 45-degree diamond, dead-centre, plus in some seeds two small lighter squares set side by side inside the square (101, 249, 323, 434, 212, 508) and in others two-to-four diamonds overlapping around a shared centre (138, 286, 360, 397, 471). There is no vertical stack anywhere on the contact sheet: no course boundaries, no diminishing courses toward a top, no asymmetry of weight, no base resting on anything, no ground plane, no weathering, no edge irregularity. Every form is a perfect hard-edged Euclidean polygon with uniform flat fill. The diamond seeds read as a compass rose or a quadrant diagram; the square-with-two-inner-squares seeds read, unfortunately and consistently, as a face. Seed 175 in particular is one uniform grey diamond on black at all three states -- a rotated square, nothing more. This is not a competent cairn or an abstracted cairn; it is a different subject entirely.
critique.action: Rebuild the primitive as a vertical stack, not a centred polygon. Generate 4-7 horizontal courses stacked bottom-to-top along a single vertical axis, each course a separate quadrilateral; taper course width monotonically from roughly 100% at the base to 25-35% at the cap so the silhouette narrows upward and reads as one object with a top and a bottom. Jitter each course's horizontal centre by 3-8% of stack width and its top/bottom edges by 1-3 degrees so the stack leans and the joints are not flush. Perturb every course outline with 5-9 vertices off the rectangle so the edges are chipped rather than ruled. Seat the base on a horizon or shadow at roughly 78-84% of frame height so the object stands rather than floats. Remove the 45-degree diamond form entirely -- it is the single strongest reason this reads as compass geometry -- and remove the paired-inner-square motif, which produces a face.

critique.observation: The state sheets deliver no change at all. In states.png the three tiles of each row (101, 138, 175, 212) are visually identical: same silhouette, same scale, same fill values, same position, same count of elements. In states-thumb.png all twelve seeds are shown across all three rows and every column is three copies of one tile -- I cannot identify which row is neutral, which is stress and which is recovery from the pictures alone; only the captions distinguish them. The three seed-175 single frames are likewise indistinguishable from one another down to the pixel. The brief claims the stack loses courses and reads as precarious under drawdown and rebuilds on recovery. Nothing is lost, nothing tilts, nothing rebuilds. This is precisely the failure the rubric names: a state transition invisible on the sheet has not been delivered.
critique.action: Bind course count and stack geometry to the market state and make the delta large enough to survive 120px. Under stress, drop 40-60% of the courses (a 6-course stack should render as 2-3), increase the lean of the surviving cap course to 8-15 degrees off vertical, widen the joint gaps to 2-4% of stack height so daylight shows between stones, and let one displaced course sit fallen at the base. Under recovery, restore full course count but leave 1-2 courses visibly re-seated -- offset and slightly darker -- so recovery is legibly a rebuild rather than a reset to neutral. Also shift the ground value between states (stress ground 10-15% darker, recovery ground warmer) so the row is distinguishable even before the stack is parsed. The single test to pass: strip the captions from states-thumb.png and a stranger should still be able to name which row is the drawdown.

critique.observation: Twelve seeds resolve to two motifs. Motif A is an axis-aligned grey square containing two small lighter squares (101, 249, 323, 434, and 212/508 as square-ish variants). Motif B is one or more 45-degree diamonds sharing a centre (138, 175, 286, 360, 397, 471). Within each motif the differences are rotation, count and scale only -- 138, 360 and 471 are the same four-diamond cluster at different sizes and overlap opacities; 101, 249, 323 and 434 differ only in the base square's value and the inner squares' spacing. Seed 286 and seed 397 are the same small diamond cluster at two brightnesses. This is one work at twelve settings, not twelve works.
critique.action: Move the variation into structural parameters that change the silhouette rather than the transform. Vary course count 3-8, base-to-cap taper ratio 0.2-0.6, lean direction and magnitude, whether the cap is a single flat capstone or a small pointed stone, and whether a second smaller satellite cairn stands in the field at 20-35% of the main stack's height. Cap the shared-geometry rate: no two of the twelve seeds should have both the same course count and the same taper bracket. Fix the current failure mode by deleting the transform-only variation path -- rotation and uniform scale must not be the primary seed axes.

critique.observation: At 120px in contact-thumb.png the tiles are legible as shapes -- they are large and sit high against a near-black ground -- but they do not read as twelve things. They collapse to roughly three stamps: light square with two dots, light diamond, small dark diamond cluster. Seed 397 is so low in value that it very nearly disappears into the ground at this size; it reads as an almost-empty tile. Seed 508's form fills nearly the whole tile and touches the frame, so its silhouette is lost and it reads as a flat grey rectangle. The internal overlaps that carry most of the differentiation at 512px (the translucent seams in 138, 360, 471) fall below the threshold of visibility at 120px, which is exactly why the sheet flattens.
critique.action: Design at 120px first. Ensure every seed's silhouette is distinguishable from every other seed's by outline alone with all interior detail removed -- test this by rendering the collection as solid black shapes on white and checking that no two are confusable. Raise seed 397's form value to at least 35-40% luminance above the ground so no tile reads as empty. Constrain every form to 60-72% of tile width so a margin of empty field always frames the object (this also serves the brief's 'standing alone in an empty field'). Stop relying on translucent overlaps for differentiation; they are invisible below about 200px.

critique.observation: Every frame is a single form centred on both axes with near-symmetric margins, floating with no ground, no horizon and no scale cue. There is dominance -- one object clearly leads -- but no hierarchy inside the object: the interior is one flat fill, or one flat fill plus two equal-weight inner squares that compete with each other and with nothing else. The frame is not used; the composition would be unchanged if the canvas were square, portrait or landscape. In seed 212 the inner light rectangle overhangs the left edge of the base square and the whole assembly sits off-centre against its own darker backing block, which reads as a misregistration rather than a decision. In seed 508 the form runs off the right and bottom of the tile.
critique.action: Introduce a ground and an off-centre placement. Seat the stack on a horizon line at 78-84% of frame height and offset the stack's vertical axis 8-15% from centre so the empty field is asymmetric and the object has somewhere to stand. Build hierarchy into the object by making the base course the largest and darkest mass and the cap the smallest and lightest, with a 2.5:1 or greater area ratio between them, so the eye climbs the stack. Keep the form inside 60-72% of frame width so the surrounding field is genuinely empty rather than crowded.

critique.observation: The brief names four mineral families -- granite grey, lichen green-grey, iron oxide, bone. What renders is essentially one warm neutral grey around 55-62% luminance with a faint khaki cast, sitting on a near-black ground around 8-10%, with the only other values being slightly lighter or darker mixes of that same grey where shapes overlap. There is no green anywhere, no oxide red anywhere, and no bone -- the lightest note (seed 434, seed 508) is the same khaki grey pushed brighter. The colour reads as an untinted default greyscale rather than as chosen mineral. The contrast range is also badly distributed: almost all of it is spent on the single figure/ground step, and almost none on the internal structure, so the ground supports the drawing but the drawing has no internal reading at all. Seed 397 falls the other way and nearly loses figure/ground entirely.
critique.action: Build a four-stop mineral ramp and actually spend it: granite grey around 45% luminance, lichen green-grey with a real green bias (hue near 90-110 degrees, 8-14% saturation), iron oxide with a real red-orange bias (hue near 15-25 degrees, 20-30% saturation), and bone at 78-85% luminance with a warm cast. Assign each course a stop so the stack has internal value steps of at least 12-15% luminance between adjacent courses -- that is what will make the courses read as separate stones at 120px. Restrict oxide to one or two courses per token as an accent so it stays weathering and does not become decoration. Lift the ground off near-black to a low mineral value around 15-18% so it reads as field rather than void.

critique.observation: The twelve tiles do read as one project. Shared ground value, shared flat hard-edged geometric vocabulary, shared centred placement and a shared narrow grey palette bind them convincingly on the contact sheet. This is the one axis the work clearly passes -- though it passes partly for the wrong reason: the tiles are coherent because they are so similar to one another, which is the same fact that fails seedVariation. Coherence here is currently a symptom of sameness, not of a shared system that admits difference.
critique.action: Preserve the shared ground, the shared palette ramp and the shared silhouette logic when you widen the structural variation above -- those three are what will keep the collection coherent once the tokens stop being near-copies. Do not add a second rendering style or a second ground treatment to create variety; get the variety from course count, taper, lean and satellite stones inside the one system.

critique.observation: Same seed across the three states is unambiguously the same token -- in fact it is the identical image, which I confirmed by looking at seeds 101, 138, 175 and 212 in states.png and at all twelve columns in states-thumb.png. The axis's stated failure mode (a token replaced by a different object under drawdown) does not occur. This is a pass, but a vacuous one: identity is preserved because nothing happens, not because a changing object holds its identity while changing.
critique.action: When you implement the state response, hold identity by keeping three things invariant across states: the base course's outline and position, the token's colour-stop assignment, and the stack's lean direction. Vary only course count, joint gaps, lean magnitude and ground value. That keeps the same object recognisable through a real transformation rather than through the absence of one.

critique.observation: Named and located: (1) seed 508, bottom-right of contact.png and contact-thumb.png -- the form runs off the right edge and the bottom edge of the tile and is cut by the viewBox, so its silhouette is destroyed and it reads as a flat rectangle. (2) Seed 212, top row of contact.png and all three states in states.png -- the light inner rectangle overhangs the left edge of the darker base block and the horizontal bands do not align to it, reading as a registration error rather than a composed overlap. (3) Seed 138, visible in states.png at all three states -- a small notch or nick at the upper-left of the top diamond where two overlapping diamonds meet, a hairline seam artifact at the vertex. (4) Seed 397 -- the form's value is so close to the ground that at 120px the tile reads as nearly empty; the stroke effectively vanishes. (5) Across 138, 286, 360 and 471 the translucent overlap regions produce a lattice of faint quadrant seams that reads as a rendering byproduct rather than as drawn structure.
critique.action: Clamp every form to a bounding box of at most 72% of the tile in each dimension so nothing can reach the viewBox edge. Snap overlapping shape vertices to a shared grid or merge the shapes into a single path before fill so coincident edges cannot produce hairline notches. Enforce a minimum figure/ground luminance separation of 25% so no seed can render near-invisible. Replace alpha-blended overlaps with explicit opaque course fills drawn back-to-front -- the current translucency is generating structure nobody chose.

critique.observation: There is still no cairn anywhere on the contact sheet. The colour changed since the last look -- everything is now a warm terracotta on a dark-to-sand vertical gradient instead of grey on black -- but the subject did not. Every one of the twelve tiles is a single large axis-aligned terracotta square, roughly centred, with a small pale square near its middle; four of them (138, 175, 360, 471) add a 45-degree grey diamond whose four points poke out at the exact cardinal midpoints, and four (212, 249, 323, 434) add a grey backing frame. I count zero horizontal courses, zero course boundaries, zero taper, zero lean, zero capstone, zero base, zero horizon, and zero weathered or irregular edges in the whole packet -- every outline is a ruled Euclidean polygon with a flat or alpha-blended fill. The brief's 'one stacked cairn standing alone in an empty field, weathered and heavy, a single object with a top and a bottom' is not present in any seed. What 175, 101 and 212 actually read as is a framed photograph or a Polaroid; 138, 360 and 471, with their four-way symmetric diamond points, read as a compass rosette, which the brief explicitly rules out ('not a mandala'). Seeds 101, 138, 175, 360, 471 and 508 additionally scatter 4-14 small oxide chips across the square face, which is the 'ornament' the brief also rules out.
critique.action: Delete the centred-polygon primitive and the 45-degree diamond overlay entirely, and rebuild the token as a vertical stack: emit 4-7 separate quadrilateral courses stacked bottom-to-top on one vertical axis, each course's width tapering monotonically from 100% at the base to 25-35% at the cap, with each course outline perturbed to 5-9 vertices so no edge is ruled. Give each course 1-3 degrees of independent tilt and offset its horizontal centre by 3-8% of stack width so the joints are not flush. Seat the base on a horizon line at 78-84% of frame height. Remove the scattered small oxide chips from the square face in all six seeds that carry them (101, 138, 175, 360, 471, 508) -- cap decorative marks at 0 and let all incident come from course edges and joints.

critique.observation: singles--seed175-neutral.png and singles--seed175-stress.png are the same picture. I compared them side by side and could find no difference in the square, the diamond, the two interior blocks, the four oxide chips or the ground; a byte comparison confirms the two files are identical. Recovery differs from both by exactly one thing: the pale bone square left of centre is about 15% wider and the dark grey chip inside it is about 40% larger. Across the whole of states.png the same single delta is the only change in all four rows -- in 101, 138, 175 and 212 the interior pale square grows monotonically neutral < stress < recovery and nothing else moves. That means stress and recovery are not even different in kind, only in degree along one axis, and the brief's claim is the opposite: stress should LOSE courses and read precarious, recovery should REBUILD. Nothing is lost, nothing tilts, nothing gains a gap, nothing re-seats. In states-thumb.png at 120px the three rows are indistinguishable to me without reading the captions.
critique.action: Bind course count and joint geometry to the state, not one interior square's scale. Under stress drop 40-60% of the courses (a 6-course stack renders as 2-3), tilt the surviving cap course 8-15 degrees off vertical, open the joints to 2-4% of stack height so ground shows between stones, and lay one displaced course fallen at the base. Under recovery restore the full course count but leave 1-2 courses visibly re-seated -- offset 5-10% and one palette stop darker -- so recovery reads as a rebuild and not a reset. Shift the ground too: stress ground 10-15% darker, recovery ground warmer by 8-12 degrees of hue. The acceptance test is the one that failed here: strip the captions from states-thumb.png and a stranger must still be able to point at the drawdown row.

critique.observation: At 120px in contact-thumb.png the twelve tiles collapse to one stamp: an orange square with a small pale square near its centre. Every differentiating feature I can name at 512px falls below threshold here -- the grey diamond behind 138, 175, 360 and 471 survives only as four faint nicks at the square's edge midpoints and reads as damage rather than as a second form; the scattered oxide chips in 101, 360, 471 and 508 dissolve into faint mottling; the olive interior diamond in 175 becomes an indistinct smudge. The only tiles I can name blind are 434 (thick grey border), 212 (light frame with a row of dots along the top) and 508 (fills the tile). That is 3 of 12 identifiable. Worse, the bottom third of most tiles is pale sand ground that is brighter than any part of the object, so at browse size the eye lands on empty background rather than the form.
critique.action: Design at 120px first and test on silhouette alone: render all twelve tokens as solid black shapes on white with every interior mark removed, and require that no two of the twelve be confusable by outline -- the current set would give one shape twelve times. Get the differentiation from the stack's outline (course count 3-8, taper ratio 0.2-0.6, lean direction and magnitude, flat capstone versus pointed cap, presence of a satellite stack at 20-35% of main height), not from interior chips or translucent overlays, which are invisible below about 200px. Cap the ground's top-to-bottom luminance ramp at 25 points and keep its brightest value at least 15 points below the object's lightest course, so no tile's background outshines its subject.

critique.observation: Twelve seeds resolve to three templates and one silhouette. Template A is a bare terracotta square with a centre bone chip (286, 397, 508, and 101 with extra interior blocks); template B is the same square with a 45-degree grey diamond behind it (138, 175, 360, 471); template C is the same square inside a grey backing frame (212, 249, 323, 434). Inside each template the only things that move are scale, the frame's grey value and the bone chip's position -- 249, 323 and 434 differ only in how thick and how light the surrounding frame is, and 138, 360 and 471 are the same square-plus-diamond at three sizes with the chip cluster rotated. 286 and 397 are the same tile at two square sizes. This is one work at twelve settings.
critique.action: Move variation onto parameters that change the outline rather than the transform: vary course count across the full 3-8 range, base-to-cap taper across 0.2-0.6, lean direction and magnitude, cap type, and whether a satellite stack stands in the field. Enforce a constraint that no two of the twelve seeds share both the same course count and the same taper bracket. Delete the scale-only and frame-thickness-only variation paths that currently produce 249/323/434 and 286/397 -- uniform scale must not be a seed axis at all.

critique.observation: Every frame is one form centred on both axes and floating. There is no ground plane and no horizon -- the background is a smooth top-to-bottom gradient from near-black to pale sand, and the object's bottom edge simply stops partway down it with nothing to stand on, so nothing has weight and there is no scale cue. Inside the object the hierarchy is inverted: the largest mass is a single flat fill with no internal reading, and the only focal accent is a small pale square with a dark dot in it sitting at or near dead centre, which reads as a bullseye or a shutter. In 175 that pale block and the olive diamond to its right sit at the same height and the same size and read as a pair of eyes. The gradient background carries a wider luminance range than anything inside the form, so the loudest tonal event in most tiles is empty field. The frame is unused -- these compositions would be unchanged in a square, portrait or landscape canvas.
critique.action: Seat the stack on a horizon or contact shadow at 78-84% of frame height and offset its vertical axis 8-15% from centre so the empty field is asymmetric. Build the hierarchy into the stack: make the base course the largest and darkest mass and the cap the smallest and lightest, with an area ratio of at least 2.5:1 between them, so the eye climbs from bottom to top instead of stopping at a centred chip. Remove the centred pale-square-with-dark-dot motif from all twelve seeds -- it is what makes 175 and 101 read as a face. Constrain the object to 60-72% of tile width so a genuine empty margin frames it.

critique.observation: Named and located. (1) Seed 508, bottom-right of contact.png and contact-thumb.png: the form spans nearly the whole tile, its left and right edges land within a few pixels of the border, and the top row of small light and oxide squares is clipped by the object's own top edge -- the silhouette is destroyed and at 120px it is a flat rectangle. (2) Seed 212, contact.png and all three states of states.png: a green rectangle and a grey block both protrude past the top-left of the terracotta square while the row of six small chips along the top overhangs the square's top edge -- it reads as misregistration, not as a composed overlap. (3) Seed 249, contact.png: a thin green vertical strip pokes out from behind the square's right edge at an arbitrary height, reading as a leaked layer. (4) Seeds 138, 175, 360, 471: the alpha-blended diamond over the square produces four differently-valued triangular quadrants and a lighter central lozenge -- a seam lattice nobody drew -- and the diamond's four points emerge exactly at the square's edge midpoints, which is what makes these read as compass geometry. (5) Seeds 323 and 434, lower half: the grey backing frame drops to within a few percent of the pale ground behind it, so its bottom edge disappears and the object looks cut off. (6) Seed 101: the dark chip is a loose 3px dot floating on the orange above the bone square in neutral, and becomes a distinct grey square attached to it in recovery -- the same element changes kind, not just size, between states.
critique.action: Clamp every form to at most 72% of the tile in each dimension so nothing can reach the viewBox edge, which fixes 508. Replace all alpha-blended overlaps with opaque fills drawn back-to-front and merge coincident shapes into a single path before filling, which removes the quadrant seam lattice in 138/175/360/471. Enforce a minimum 25-point luminance separation between any object edge and the ground directly behind it at that height, which fixes the vanishing frame bottoms in 323 and 434. Clip or delete the stray protruding strips in 212 and 249 -- no element may extend past the primary mass unless it is a deliberate course offset.

critique.observation: This moved since the last look and it is the only axis that did. All four named families are now at least nominally present: granite grey in the backing frames of 212, 249, 323 and 434 and in the diamond overlays, bone in the small pale interior squares, iron oxide as the dominant field, lichen green as a thin strip left of the square in 212 and right of it in 249 and as a faint diamond in 471. But the allocation is wrong for the brief. Iron oxide is not an accent here -- it is roughly 60-70% of the picture area in every tile, at a saturation that reads as new terracotta tile or brick rather than weathered mineral, and the brief asks for muted with nothing bright. Lichen green appears in 3 of 12 tiles and only as an artifact of something protruding from behind, never as a chosen surface. And the contrast range is spent in the wrong place: the ground gradient runs from near-black at the top to pale sand at the bottom, a wider range than exists anywhere inside the object, whose interior is one flat fill plus one bone chip. The ground competes with the drawing and in the lower third it wins.
critique.action: Invert the allocation. Make granite grey around 45% luminance the dominant course colour, restrict iron oxide to 1-2 courses per token as weathering accent, give lichen green a real assignment as a course or as a patch on the base course in at least 6 of 12 seeds rather than a leaked strip, and keep bone at 78-85% luminance for the cap. Spend the contrast inside the object: adjacent courses must differ by at least 12-15 luminance points so they read as separate stones at 120px. Flatten the ground to a low mineral value around 15-18% with a total ramp of no more than 25 points, so it reads as field rather than as the brightest thing in the frame.

critique.observation: The twelve tiles unmistakably read as one project. A shared ground gradient, a shared flat hard-edged geometric vocabulary, a shared centred placement, a shared terracotta field and a shared bone chip bind the contact sheet convincingly. This is the axis the work passes -- but it passes for the same reason seedVariation fails: the tiles cohere because they are near-copies of one another, so coherence here is a symptom of sameness rather than of a system that admits difference.
critique.action: Hold exactly three things constant when you widen the structural variation -- the ground treatment, the four-stop mineral ramp, and the stacked-course silhouette logic -- and let course count, taper, lean and satellite stones carry all the difference. Do not add a second rendering style, a second ground treatment or a second geometric vocabulary to manufacture variety; that would trade this pass for a new failure.

critique.observation: Same seed across three states is unambiguously the same token -- I checked 101, 138, 175 and 212 in states.png and all twelve columns in states-thumb.png. Nothing is replaced, nothing swaps motif, nothing changes silhouette. But this is a vacuous pass, exactly as it was before: identity holds because seed 175's neutral and stress frames are literally the same image and recovery differs by one interior square's size. Identity is preserved by the absence of change, not by a changing object holding together.
critique.action: When you implement the real state response, hold identity by keeping three things invariant across all three states: the base course's outline and position, the token's assignment of the four palette stops, and the lean direction. Let only course count, joint gap, lean magnitude and ground value vary. That preserves this pass through an actual transformation instead of through stillness.

critique.observation: There is still no cairn in this packet, and the third look makes the reason precise rather than impressionistic. Every one of the twelve tiles on contact.png is a single axis-aligned terracotta square, roughly filling the middle of the frame, carrying one small bone-coloured square near its centre. Four seeds (138, 175, 360, 471) sit a 45-degree diamond over that square whose four points emerge exactly at the square's edge midpoints; four (212, 249, 323, 434) set the square inside a flat grey backing frame; the rest are the bare square. I stripped every interior mark and looked at the twelve outlines alone: nine of the twelve are a plain filled square, 138 and 471 are an eight-pointed star, and 508 is a square clipped by the tile border. The object is never taller than it is wide -- the height/width ratio of the twelve silhouettes runs 0.84 to 1.00, and eight of them are exactly 1.00 -- and the silhouette is mirror-symmetric top-to-bottom in ten of twelve seeds. A cairn is by definition asymmetric between its top and its bottom; a shape that is identical when flipped cannot read as one. I count zero horizontal courses, zero joints, zero taper, zero lean, zero capstone, zero base and zero horizon in the entire packet. What 101, 212, 249 and 397 actually read as is a framed photograph or a monitor with a screen in it; what 138 and 471 read as is a compass rosette, which the brief rules out by name.
critique.action: Delete the centred-square primitive and the 45-degree diamond overlay from the generator entirely, and emit instead 4-7 separate quadrilateral courses stacked bottom-to-top on one vertical axis. Taper course width monotonically from 100% at the base to 25-35% at the cap, and size the stack so its silhouette bounding box is 1.5:1 to 2.2:1 tall (it is 1.00:1 today in eight of twelve seeds). Perturb every course outline to 5-9 vertices so no edge is ruled, give each course 1-3 degrees of independent tilt and 3-8% horizontal offset so the joints are not flush, and seat the base course on a horizon or contact shadow at 78-84% of frame height. The acceptance test is the one this round fails: render the twelve as solid black outlines with all interior marks removed and require that no silhouette match its own vertical mirror above 60% -- ten of twelve currently match at 100%.

critique.observation: singles--seed175-neutral.png and singles--seed175-recovery.png are the same picture -- I compared them and could find no difference in the square, the diamond, the bone block, the dark chip or the ground, and they are byte-identical files. The stress frame differs from both by exactly one thing: a single small oxide chip roughly 10px across appears at the lower-left corner of the bone square. Across states.png the story is the same in all four rows: the whole assembly rescales by one or two percent and one interior chip grows or appears; in 138 stress a small oxide diamond block turns on at the upper left, in 212 stress one extra pale block appears beside the bone chip. Nothing is lost, nothing tilts, no gap opens, nothing is re-seated, and the ground value is identical in all three columns. I measured the change at browse size on states-thumb.png: stress alters 3.2% to 5.8% of the tile's pixels in ten of the twelve seeds. Worse for the brief's story, recovery differs from neutral MORE than stress does in ten of twelve seeds (175: 8.2% vs 5.5%; 249: 8.5% vs 5.4%; 360: 8.4% vs 5.8%), so the sequence does not settle back -- it drifts further out. In states-thumb.png I cannot name which of the three rows is the drawdown without reading the captions.
critique.action: Bind course count and joint geometry to the state instead of one interior chip's size. Under stress drop 40-60% of the courses so a 6-course stack renders as 2 or 3, tilt the surviving cap course 8-15 degrees off vertical, open the joints to 2-4% of stack height so ground shows between the stones, and lay one displaced course fallen at the base. Under recovery restore the full course count but leave 1-2 courses visibly re-seated -- offset 5-10% and one palette stop darker -- so the rebuild is legible as a rebuild. Also move the ground: stress ground 10-15% darker, recovery ground 8-12 degrees warmer in hue. Target a pixel delta above 25% at 120px between neutral and stress, against the 3-6% measured here, and require neutral-to-recovery to be SMALLER than neutral-to-stress in at least 10 of 12 seeds -- it is larger in 10 of 12 today. Fix the seed-175 singles first: neutral and recovery must not be the same file.

critique.observation: At 120px in contact-thumb.png the twelve tiles collapse to one stamp -- a terracotta square with a small pale chip. The grey diamonds behind 138, 175, 360 and 471 survive only as four faint nicks at the square's edge midpoints and read as chipped corners rather than as a second form; the ghost diamonds inside 286, 397 and 508 sit within about 8 luminance points of the field and dissolve completely; the dark chip inside the bone square in 249, 397 and 508 becomes a single indistinct dot. The only three tiles I can name blind at this size are 434 (thin grey border around a small square), 323 (thick grey border) and 508 (form fills the tile edge to edge). That is 3 of 12 identifiable, unchanged from the previous look. The differentiating information is all interior and all below threshold; the outlines, which are what survives, are nine copies of one square.
critique.action: Move every differentiating decision into the outline and test it at 120px before rendering anything at 512px. Vary course count across the full 3-8 range, base-to-cap taper across 0.2-0.6, lean direction and magnitude, flat capstone versus pointed cap, and the presence of a satellite stack at 20-35% of main height. Delete the interior ghost diamonds in 286, 397 and 508 and the interior chip-inside-a-chip motif in 249, 397 and 508 -- both are invisible below about 200px and are currently carrying differentiation they cannot deliver. Require 10 of 12 tiles to be nameable from outline alone at 120px, against the 3 of 12 measured here.

critique.observation: Twelve seeds resolve to three templates over one silhouette, and the templates are the same three as before. Template A is a bare terracotta square with a bone chip (101, 286, 397); template B is that square with a 45-degree grey diamond behind it (138, 175, 360, 471); template C is that square inside a grey backing frame (212, 249, 323, 434). Inside each template the only things that move are uniform scale, the frame's grey value and the bone chip's quadrant. 323 and 434 differ only in the frame's thickness and lightness. 286 and 397 are the same tile at two sizes with the chip moved from upper-left to upper-right. 138 and 471 are the same square-plus-diamond assembly at two scales. I measured the object's bounding box across all twelve: the widths run 52% to 92% of the tile and the aspect ratio runs 0.84 to 1.00, so uniform scale is doing almost all of the visible work.
critique.action: Delete uniform scale and frame-thickness as seed axes -- they are what produce the 323/434 and 286/397 duplicates. Replace them with structural axes that change the outline: course count 3-8, taper ratio 0.2-0.6, lean direction and magnitude, cap type, satellite stack present or absent. Enforce a hard constraint that no two of the twelve seeds share both the same course count and the same taper bracket, and clamp every object's bounding box to 60-72% of tile width so scale can no longer be a variation channel at all (five seeds exceed that today: 249 at 81%, 323 at 78%, 471 at 90%, 508 at 92%, 286 at 73%).

critique.observation: I measured the bounding-box centre of all twelve objects against the tile centre: every single one is dead centre, with horizontal offsets between -2.4% and +0.6% and vertical offsets between -3.0% and +1.6%. Twelve of twelve. There is no ground plane and no horizon anywhere -- the background is a smooth vertical gradient and the object's bottom edge simply stops on it with nothing to stand on, so nothing has weight and there is no scale cue. Inside the object the hierarchy is inverted: the largest mass, the terracotta square, is one flat fill with no internal reading, and the only focal accent is a small bone square placed near the middle, often with a dark chip inside it. In 249 and 508 that bone square with a dark grey square inside it reads unmistakably as a window or a screen; in 212 the bone chip with a dark dot sits in the upper-left quadrant beside a green block and reads as an eye. The frame is unused -- every one of these compositions would be unchanged in a square, portrait or landscape canvas.
critique.action: Offset each stack's vertical axis 8-15% from the tile centre so the empty field is asymmetric, and seat the base on a horizon or contact shadow at 78-84% of frame height -- both were asked for twice and the measured offset is still under 3% in all twelve. Build the hierarchy into the stack by making the base course the largest and darkest mass and the cap the smallest and lightest, with an area ratio of at least 2.5:1 between them, so the eye climbs from bottom to top. Remove the bone-square-containing-a-dark-square motif from all twelve seeds -- it is what makes 249 and 508 read as a monitor and 212 as a face.

critique.observation: This is the one axis that moved and the movement is real but partial. The ground is fixed: it now runs from about 22% luminance at the top of a tile down to 8% at the bottom, a 14-point ramp with the darkest value at the base, and the object's lightest note (bone, at 69%) now clearly out-values every part of the field. The pale sand that used to outshine the subject is gone. Granite grey has also arrived as a genuine mass rather than a leak -- it is 38% of the object area in 323, 29% in 212, 24% in 249 and 18% in 434. But the allocation is still wrong for the brief in two specific ways. Iron oxide averages 34% of object area across the twelve and is 62% in 286 and 56% in 508; it is the field, not the accent, and at that saturation it reads as new terracotta tile rather than weathered mineral. Lichen green-grey averages 1.0% of object area and clears 4% in only two seeds (212 and 508), and in both it is the leaked strip protruding from behind the square's edge, never a chosen surface. Contrast is also still spent almost entirely on the figure-ground step: the terracotta mass is one flat fill, so there are no internal value steps for courses to read against.
critique.action: Invert the allocation. Make granite grey at roughly 45% luminance the dominant course colour, cut iron oxide to 1-2 courses per token so it lands under 15% of object area (it is 34% today, 62% in 286), and give lichen green-grey a real assignment as a course fill or a patch on the base course in at least 6 of 12 seeds rather than the protruding strip in 212 and 249. Keep bone at 78-85% luminance for the cap only. Then spend the contrast inside the object: adjacent courses must differ by at least 12-15 luminance points so they separate as stones at 120px. Keep the current ground -- the 14-point ramp darkening toward the base is correct and should not be touched.

critique.observation: Named and located. (1) Seed 508, bottom-right of contact.png and contact-thumb.png: the object spans 92% of tile width and 83% of height, its terracotta mass sits within a few pixels of the left and right tile borders, and the green strip on its right side is cut by the tile edge -- at 120px the silhouette is destroyed and it reads as a flat rectangle. (2) Seed 212, top row of contact.png and all three states of states.png: a green rectangle and a smaller olive block protrude past the left edge of the terracotta mass, and the terracotta itself is built from two offset rectangles whose seam runs as a visible step across the upper left -- it reads as misregistration, not as a composed overlap. (3) Seed 249: the same green strip leaks from behind the square's left edge at an arbitrary height, and the grey backing frame reaches 81% of tile width. (4) Seeds 138, 175, 360 and 471: the alpha-blended diamonds over the square generate six to eight differently-valued triangular quadrants and a lighter central lozenge -- a seam lattice nobody drew -- and the diamond points emerge exactly at the square's edge midpoints, which is what produces the compass-rosette silhouette. (5) Seed 138 and seed 286: the dark chip attached to the bone square overhangs the bone square's own edge onto the terracotta beneath, and in 138 the bone square's right edge overhangs the terracotta square's right edge by about 3px. (6) Seed 101: a lone dark blue-grey dot roughly 4px across floats above the bone square, attached to nothing, reading as a dead pixel; the same tile carries a ghost rectangle in its lower right that sits within about 8 luminance points of the field and reads as a compression block rather than a drawn form.
critique.action: Clamp every form to at most 72% of the tile in each dimension so nothing can reach the viewBox edge -- that fixes 508 at 92% and 471 at 90%. Replace all alpha-blended overlaps with opaque fills drawn back to front and merge coincident shapes into one path before filling, which removes the quadrant seam lattice in 138, 175, 360 and 471. Clip or delete the protruding green strips in 212, 249 and 508 -- no element may extend past the primary mass unless it is a deliberate course offset. Delete the 4px floating dot in 101 and the ghost rectangles in 101, 286 and 397, and enforce a minimum 12-point luminance separation for any mark that is meant to be seen so nothing renders as a compression artifact.

critique.observation: The twelve tiles unmistakably read as one project. A shared vertical ground gradient, a shared hard-edged flat-fill geometric vocabulary, a shared dead-centre placement, a shared terracotta field and a shared bone chip bind the contact sheet convincingly, and the state sheets do not break it. This is the axis the work passes -- but it passes for the same reason seedVariation fails: the tiles cohere because they are near-copies, so coherence here is a symptom of sameness rather than of a system that admits difference.
critique.action: Hold exactly three things constant when you widen the structural variation -- the current ground gradient, the four-stop mineral ramp and the stacked-course silhouette logic -- and let course count, taper, lean and satellite stones carry all of the difference. Do not add a second rendering style, a second ground treatment or a second geometric vocabulary to manufacture variety; that would trade this pass for a new failure.

critique.observation: Same seed across three states is unambiguously the same token. I checked 101, 138, 175 and 212 in states.png and all twelve columns in states-thumb.png: nothing is replaced, nothing swaps motif, no silhouette changes. But this is a vacuous pass for the third time -- identity holds because seed 175's neutral and recovery frames are literally the same image and its stress frame adds one 10px chip. Identity is preserved by the absence of change, not by a changing object holding together.
critique.action: When you implement the real state response, hold identity by keeping three things invariant across all three states: the base course's outline and position, the token's assignment of the four palette stops, and the lean direction. Let only course count, joint gap, lean magnitude and ground value vary. That preserves this pass through an actual transformation instead of through stillness.

critique.observation: There is no cairn in this packet, and this time I settled it by outline rather than by impression. I thresholded contact.png at the figure/ground step and looked at the twelve silhouettes with every interior mark gone: 101, 212, 249, 323, 434 and 508 are a plain filled square; 175 and 360 are a plain diamond; 138 and 471 are a diamond with one or two small bumps on the upper edge; 286 and 397 are a ragged square blob. Six squares and five diamonds. Not one of the twelve is taller than it is wide, and every one of the twelve is mirror-symmetric top-to-bottom, which a stacked marker cannot be — a cairn's whole subject is that its bottom is not its top. I count zero horizontal courses, zero joints, zero taper, zero lean, zero capstone, zero base, zero horizon and zero weathered or irregular edges in all seven images. Every outline is a ruled Euclidean polygon. What the tiles actually read as: 249 is a face (two oxide blocks with bone pupils sitting side by side at the same height on a green band, with the band running out to left and right as ears); 101 is the same face at lower contrast; 138 carries a faint green vertical and horizontal line crossing the diamond plus two orange plus-marks, which is a reticle; 508 is a 2x2 quadrant grid of nested squares with two orange crosshairs at its centre, which is a targeting display or a quadtree diagram; 175, 286, 360, 397 and 471 are eight-pointed rosettes, the mandala the brief rules out by name.
critique.action: Delete the centred-square primitive and the 45-degree diamond overlay from the generator — they produce eleven of the twelve silhouettes — and emit instead 4-7 separate quadrilateral courses stacked bottom-to-top on one vertical axis. Taper course width monotonically from 100% at the base to 25-35% at the cap and size the stack so its silhouette bounding box is 1.5:1 to 2.2:1 TALL; it is 1.0:1 or wider in all twelve today. Perturb every course outline to 5-9 vertices so no edge is ruled, give each course 1-3 degrees of independent tilt and 3-8% horizontal offset so joints are not flush, and seat the base course on a horizon or contact shadow at 78-84% of frame height. Delete the two orange plus-marks in 138 and the two in 508, and delete the faint green crossed lines in 138 — those four marks are why the set reads as an instrument. Acceptance test, unchanged from the last look and still failed 12 of 12: render the twelve as solid black shapes on white and require that no silhouette match its own vertical mirror above 60%.

critique.observation: The state response is now visible, and it is pointed the wrong way. I built a neutral-over-stress strip from states-thumb.png and a neutral-over-recovery strip from the same sheet and compared them column by column at browse size. Stress is indistinguishable from neutral in 101, 138, 175, 360, 397 and 434, and differs only by chips shifting a few pixels in 212, 249, 323 and 471 — eight to ten of twelve. Recovery, by contrast, departs violently in all twelve: the grey backing plane drops away entirely in 101, 212, 323, 434 and 471, the green mass expands to fill the tile, and the scattered small chips consolidate into one or two large oxide blocks. Asked to point at the drawdown row with the captions covered, I would point at row 3, which is recovery. The magnitude order is inverted: neutral-to-recovery is far larger than neutral-to-stress in every seed. The shape is wrong too. The brief says the stack LOSES courses under drawdown and reads precarious; where stress does change it ADDS — 508 stress gains a row of four bone-topped oxide blocks across the top, 286 stress gains a large oxide block at bottom-centre. Nothing is lost, nothing tilts further, no joint opens, nothing falls. The only elements in the whole packet that read as a displaced stone are the fallen oxide blocks hanging off the bottom edge in 212, 397 and 175 — and all three appear in RECOVERY. And singles--seed175-neutral.png and singles--seed175-stress.png are still the same picture; I opened both and could find no difference in the diamond, the inscribed green square, the two green sub-squares, the central oxide block with its bone dot, or the ground, and the manifest gives them the same sha256. That is the third consecutive round this exact pair has shipped identical.
critique.action: Bind course count and joint geometry to the state instead of chip size and backing-plane presence. Under stress drop 40-60% of the courses so a 6-course stack renders as 2 or 3, tilt the surviving cap course 8-15 degrees off vertical, open the joints to 2-4% of stack height so ground shows between the stones, and lay one displaced course fallen at the base — move the fallen blocks currently in 212, 397 and 175 recovery into their stress frames. Under recovery restore full course count but leave 1-2 courses visibly re-seated, offset 5-10% and one palette stop darker. Reverse the measured ordering: require neutral-to-stress pixel delta above 25% at 120px against the roughly 3-6% now, and require neutral-to-recovery to be SMALLER than neutral-to-stress in at least 10 of 12 seeds — it is larger in 12 of 12 today. Fix seed 175 first: neutral and stress must not be the same file.

critique.observation: At 120px in contact-thumb.png the twelve tiles collapse to two stamps: 'grey square with a sage square in it and a few orange dots' (101, 212, 249, 323, 434, 508) and 'grey diamond with a sage shape in it and a few orange dots' (138, 175, 286, 360, 397, 471). Everything that separates them at 512px is interior and below threshold here — the nested oxide-inside-oxide chips in 508, the bone specks in 286 and 397, the faint green crosshair lines in 138, the ghost squares in 434 all dissolve. The tiles I can actually name blind at this size are 508 (a dense grid filling the tile), 286 (a small dark green mass with orange spray around its perimeter), 175 (a bare pale diamond with almost nothing on it) and 249 (two orange blocks side by side at centre). Four of twelve. 101 and 434 are the same tile to me; 360 and 471 are the same tile; 212 and 323 are the same tile. Worse, the recovery row makes this worse rather than better: 101, 212, 286, 323 and 434 recovery are five near-identical flat sage squares with one or two orange blocks, so the state the brief calls 'settle' is where the collection is least differentiated.
critique.action: Move every differentiating decision into the outline and check it at 120px before rendering anything at 512px. Vary course count across the full 3-8 range, base-to-cap taper across 0.2-0.6, lean direction and magnitude, flat capstone versus pointed cap, and presence of a satellite stack at 20-35% of main height. Delete the interior nested-chip motif in 508 and the bone specks in 286 and 397 — they are invisible below about 200px and are currently carrying differentiation they cannot deliver. Require 10 of 12 tiles nameable from outline alone at 120px, against the 4 of 12 here, and require that no two seeds in the recovery row share the same silhouette.

critique.observation: Twelve seeds resolve to two templates over two silhouettes. Template A is a flat grey plane carrying one or more sage-green squares plus scattered oxide chips: 101, 212, 249, 323, 434, 508. Template B is a pale grey 45-degree diamond with a sage square or diamond inscribed and oxide chips around it: 138, 175, 286, 360, 397, 471. Inside each template what moves is uniform scale and chip placement, nothing structural. 360 and 471 are the same diamond-plus-inscribed-square assembly at two chip densities. 101 and 434 are the same minimal grey-square-with-green-square at two sizes. 212 and 323 are the same three-square diagonal cascade, 212's compressed and 323's spread. 286 and 397 are the same green square-over-diamond star with the chip cluster rotated. The grey backing plane's width is doing much of the remaining visible work: it runs from about 50% of tile width in 434 to about 90% in 249 and 508, so scale is still a primary seed axis.
critique.action: Delete uniform scale and backing-plane width as seed axes — they are what produce the 101/434, 212/323 and 360/471 duplicates. Replace them with structural axes that change the outline: course count 3-8, taper ratio 0.2-0.6, lean direction and magnitude, cap type, satellite stack present or absent. Enforce a hard constraint that no two of the twelve share both the same course count and the same taper bracket, and clamp every object's bounding box to 60-72% of tile width so scale cannot be a variation channel at all — 249 and 508 exceed that at roughly 90% today.

critique.observation: Every one of the twelve objects sits dead centre on both axes with near-symmetric margins, and none of them stands on anything. The background is a smooth dark blue-grey vertical ramp and the object's bottom edge simply stops on it, so nothing has weight and there is no scale cue anywhere in the packet. The frame is unused — every one of these compositions would be unchanged in a square, portrait or landscape canvas. Inside the object the hierarchy is inverted: the largest mass is a flat grey or flat sage fill with no internal reading at all, and the only focal accent is a small oxide chip at or near the centre. In 323 the grey plane fills about 78% of tile width and its lower two-thirds is entirely empty — the biggest single area in that frame is a flat nothing, and the three green squares stepping diagonally through its upper half read as a staircase or a scatter plot rather than as a stack. In 249 the two oxide blocks with bone pupils are the loudest event and they sit at dead centre at the same height, which is exactly what makes that tile a face. In 138 and 508 the loudest event is a pair of orange crosshairs, also at dead centre.
critique.action: Offset each stack's vertical axis 8-15% from the tile centre so the empty field is asymmetric, and seat the base on a horizon or contact shadow at 78-84% of frame height — this has been asked for three times and the measured offset is still under 3% in all twelve. Build hierarchy into the stack by making the base course the largest and darkest mass and the cap the smallest and lightest with an area ratio of at least 2.5:1, so the eye climbs bottom to top instead of stopping at a centred chip. Remove the paired-oxide-blocks-at-equal-height motif from 249 and 101 — it is what makes them faces — and cut the empty grey plane in 323 and 434 entirely rather than leaving two-thirds of the frame as a flat fill.

critique.observation: This is the axis that moved, and the movement is real. Lichen green-grey is now the dominant surface rather than a leaked strip — it is the primary mass in all twelve tiles. Iron oxide has been demoted from field to accent and now appears as small chips rather than as 60% of the picture. Bone is present as small pale chips and pupils. Granite grey is a genuine mass as the backing plane. The ground is a low dark blue-grey ramp that the object clearly out-values everywhere, so the field no longer competes with the drawing. Nothing in the set is bright. That is four mineral stops actually deployed and actually muted. Two things still hold it back. First, the oxide is deployed as ornament: I count roughly twelve chip clusters in 508, ten in 471, nine in 286 and eight in 138, scattered across and around the mass with no structural role, and the brief says nothing decorative. Second, the contrast is still spent entirely on the figure/ground step — the dominant sage mass is one flat fill in every tile, so there are no internal value steps for anything to read as separate stones. And two marks fall below visibility: the ghost rectangles at the left and right edges of the green square in 434, and the interior ghost diamond in 397, both within a few luminance points of the fill they sit on.
critique.action: Keep the current ground ramp and the current four-stop assignment — do not touch either. Cut oxide chip count from the eight-to-twelve now in 138, 286, 471 and 508 to at most 2 per token and give each survivor a structural job as a weathered patch on one named course rather than a floating mark. Then spend the contrast inside the object: assign each course its own stop so adjacent courses differ by at least 12-15 luminance points, which is what will make them read as separate stones at 120px. Raise or delete the sub-threshold ghost rectangles in 434 and the ghost diamond in 397 — enforce a 12-point minimum luminance separation for any mark intended to be seen.

critique.observation: Named and located. (1) Seeds 138, 175, 286, 360, 397 and 471: the alpha-blended diamond over square still generates six to eight differently-valued triangular regions and a lighter central lozenge — a seam lattice nobody drew — and in 175 recovery the added dark green square's corners protrude past the diamond on all four sides, producing an eight-pointed star with eight distinct value regions. This has been present in every round. (2) Seed 286, contact.png: six oxide chips float free OUTSIDE the green mass, unattached — three above the top edge, one left, one right, one below — plus 2-3px white specks at upper left and upper right that read as dead pixels rather than as bone. (3) Seed 397: a bone chip sits detached roughly 40px below and left of the mass, attached to nothing. (4) Seed 434: pale ghost rectangles hug the left and right edges of the green square within a few luminance points of it, reading as compression blocks. (5) Seed 212: one oxide block overhangs the green mass's right edge onto the grey plane and another straddles its bottom edge, reading as misregistration rather than as a composed overlap. (6) Seed 508: the object spans roughly 90% of tile width with only a thin margin to the tile border, so at 120px its silhouette is a flat rectangle; 249 is the same at about 90%. (7) Seed 249: the two centred oxide blocks with bone pupils on a green band that extends left and right produce an unambiguous face, which is a subject artifact, not a rendering one, but it is the first thing the tile says.
critique.action: Replace every alpha-blended overlap with opaque fills drawn back-to-front and merge coincident shapes into one path before filling — that removes the seam lattice in all six diamond seeds and the eight-region star in 175 recovery. Clip or delete every element that does not touch the primary mass: the six floating chips in 286, the detached bone chip in 397, the overhanging blocks in 212. Clamp every form to at most 72% of the tile in each dimension, which fixes 508 and 249 at roughly 90%. Delete the ghost rectangles in 434 and enforce a 12-point minimum luminance separation so nothing can render as a compression block.

critique.observation: The twelve tiles unmistakably read as one project. A shared dark blue-grey ground ramp, a shared sage-over-granite flat-fill vocabulary, a shared oxide-and-bone chip language, a shared hard-edged geometry and a shared dead-centre placement bind the contact sheet convincingly, and the state sheets do not break it. This is the axis the work passes. It passes for the same reason seedVariation fails, though — the tiles cohere because they are near-copies, so coherence here is a symptom of sameness rather than of a system that admits difference.
critique.action: Hold exactly three things constant when you widen the structural variation — the current ground ramp, the current four-stop mineral assignment, and a single stacked-course silhouette logic — and let course count, taper, lean and satellite stones carry all the difference. Do not add a second rendering style, a second ground treatment or a second geometric vocabulary to manufacture variety; that would trade this pass for a new failure.

critique.observation: Same seed across three states is recognisably the same token in all twelve columns of states-thumb.png and all four rows of states.png. The diamond seeds stay diamonds through recovery, the square seeds stay squares, and the chip layout keeps its positions even when the chips grow. Nothing is replaced and no silhouette family swaps. This round the pass is no longer entirely vacuous the way it was before — recovery is a genuinely large change in every seed and identity survives it, which is the real test. It is still vacuous on the stress side, where seed 175's neutral and stress frames are literally the same image and eight of twelve seeds barely move.
critique.action: When you implement the real drawdown response, hold identity by keeping three things invariant across all three states: the base course's outline and position, the token's assignment of the four palette stops, and the lean direction. Let only course count, joint gap, lean magnitude and ground value vary. That preserves this pass through an actual transformation on the stress side instead of through stillness.

critique.observation: GATE FAIL. The brief asks for an orrery: concentric rings and dials, nested, precise, cartographic, engraved. What is on the sheet is a rosette of same-radius circles packed side by side. In seed 175 neutral and in every neutral on contact.png, the small rings are tangent and overlapping neighbours, not rings inside rings — I count essentially zero true concentric nests anywhere except the accidental double-stroke on 138. There is not one dial: no tick marks, no graduation ladder, no radial index, no numeral ring, no pointer or gnomon, nothing that reads as having been built to measure. The strokes are soft, anti-aliased and uniform in weight, which reads as painted-with-a-round-brush, not engraved; engraving needs hairline-vs-heavy weight contrast and hard terminals. The 3-fold and 6-fold rosette symmetry that organises every frame is the grammar of a flower-of-life mandala, not of an instrument — an orrery is concentric and continuous, not petalled.
critique.action: Replace the circle-scatter recursion with a concentric ring stack as the primary structure: 5-8 rings sharing ONE centre, radii stepped 8-14% apart, each ring a different stroke weight (alternate ~0.6px hairline and ~2.5px heavy). Put graduation on at least three of them — 60, 90 or 360 tick marks, ticks 4-6px long, every fifth tick doubled in length. Add one off-centre satellite dial per token at roughly 0.25 of the main radius, itself concentric. Demote the loose bubble field from primary subject to at most 15% of ink, and confine it to a single annulus between two named rings so it reads as an inscribed band rather than as foam. Kill the petal symmetry on the main armature: rings stay circular and centred; let the seed vary radii, tick counts and satellite placement instead of rosette count.

critique.observation: FAIL, and this is where the work loses decisively. On states-thumb.png the stress row is twelve near-identical stamps: pale hexagon plus one brass ring plus a handful of dots, for 101 / 212 / 249 / 323 / 360 / 397 / 434 / 471, with only 138 and 508 differing by dropping the hexagon. Twelve seeds collapse to two looks. The recovery row is worse: 101 / 138 / 212 / 249 / 286 / 323 / 360 recovery are one undifferentiated cream bubble mat at 120px and cannot be told apart at all; only the four teal-dense seeds (175, 434, 471, 508) separate. The neutral row is the best of the three and still resolves to about three clusters — a sparse hexagon family (101, 212, 249, 323, 360), a mid family (138, 286, 397) and a dense halo family (175, 434, 471, 508). On contact-thumb.png the teal disappears entirely into the brown ground, so at browse size the palette is effectively two colours, not four.
critique.action: Give each seed one silhouette-level decision that survives at 120px and is legible in ALL THREE states — vary the outer ring count between 3 and 9, vary the main-ring radius across roughly 0.45-0.9 of the frame, and vary the satellite dial's clock position. Those read as shape at thumbnail; density does not. Target: any two of the twelve stress frames distinguishable side by side at 120px. Raise the teal's value so it separates from the ground at thumbnail — lift its luminance by roughly 25-30% or it is wasted ink at browse size.

critique.observation: The change is unmistakably visible — the three rows of states-thumb.png are never confusable — so delivery is real. But the change is not the change the brief claimed, and on both ends it runs backwards. Stress is supposed to cut generations away so the instrument reads as incomplete; instead stress is the CLEANEST, most resolved, most instrument-like state in the whole packet. Seed 175 stress is a single confident brass ring with an inscribed hexagon and six satellite clusters, and it reads as finished, not wounded — 138 stress is a closed double ring with nothing broken about it. Nothing is severed, truncated, half-drawn or missing an arc anywhere in the stress row. Recovery is supposed to open the instrument out into more rings, wider; instead seed 175 recovery is a scribbled thicket of overlapping outlines that reads as steel wool, and the recovery row buries the hexagon armature under clutter rather than extending it outward.
critique.action: Invert what each state does to the STRUCTURE, not to the count. For stress, break the instrument: cut 30-50% of each ring's arc so rings render as gapped segments, drop 2-3 of the concentric rings entirely leaving visible empty radii where they were, and truncate the tick ladder mid-run. Incompleteness has to be a hole in a thing that was whole, not a smaller tidy thing. For recovery, extend outward instead of thickening inward: add rings at radii 1.1x, 1.3x and 1.5x the neutral outer ring so the instrument genuinely grows past its neutral bounds, hold total stroke count within about 130% of neutral, and forbid new marks inside the existing inner radius.

critique.observation: No focal hierarchy in two of the three states. Seed 175 neutral and 175 recovery are even fields of incident edge to edge — nothing dominates, the eye has nowhere to land, and the dark hexagonal void at centre is the only rest but it is smaller and weaker than the surrounding churn so it reads as a gap rather than as a subject. Only the stress frames have hierarchy, and they get it by subtraction. Frame use is inconsistent across the collection: 397 neutral is a small hexagon floating in the middle of an otherwise empty frame at roughly half the scale of every sibling, while 471 and 508 neutral run off all four edges. That is a 2:1 spread in occupied area between neighbours on the same sheet.
critique.action: Establish one dominant element per frame: make the primary graduated ring 1.6-2x the stroke weight and 1.3x the radius of anything else, and cap the peripheral scatter at 40% of its current density so it cannot compete. Then bound the framing — constrain the outer extent of the drawing to 0.80-0.92 of the frame half-width for every seed in neutral, so 397 grows and 471/508 pull in. A collection cannot have one member at half the scale of the rest.

critique.observation: The twelve are one work at twelve densities, not twelve works. Every seed is the same three-ingredient recipe — cream hexagon, brass circle, scatter of equal-radius rings — differing only in how much scatter is present and whether the rosette is 3-fold or 6-fold. On contact.png, 101 / 212 / 249 / 323 / 360 are interchangeable at full size, let alone at thumbnail. Nothing varies that is structural: not ring count, not radius ratio, not the presence or absence of a component, not the centre.
critique.action: Add at least two structural axes to the seed, not one density axis. Vary concentric ring count 4-9; vary the inner-to-outer radius ratio across 0.2-0.6; make the satellite dial present in only about 60% of seeds and place it at a seed-chosen clock angle; vary the inscribed polygon between triangle, square, hexagon and none. Four independent structural choices give a browsable collection; one density slider gives what is here.

critique.observation: The one axis that is clearly on-brief at full size. Aged brass ochre, oxidised copper teal, cream vellum and a warm ink-brown ground — warm metal against dark paper, exactly as asked. The ground is dark enough to carry the drawing and does not compete. Two problems. The teal sits too close to the ground in value and vanishes at 120px, so a quarter of the palette does no work at the size the collection is seen. And the cream is used at the same weight as the brass everywhere, so nothing in the colour is hierarchical — there is no accent, only three co-equal inks.
critique.action: Raise the teal's luminance by about 25-30% so it separates from the ground at thumbnail. Then make one colour the accent: restrict brass to the primary graduated ring and its ticks only, roughly 15% of ink, and let cream carry the armature. The contrast range is currently even; it should be steep.

critique.observation: Edge clipping is pervasive and does not read as deliberate bleed. Seed 175 recovery is cut by the viewBox on all four sides with a dozen circles severed mid-arc; on contact.png, 101 neutral is cut at bottom-left and right, 323 at bottom, and 471 and 508 at every edge. In seed 175 neutral there are two faint pale horizontal straight segments crossing the frame at roughly one quarter and three quarters height that have no visible partner geometry and read as stray strokes rather than as hexagon edges. At the centre of 175 recovery a small cream starburst knot forms where many strokes converge, and it reads as a rendering collision, not a drawn element. Throughout the dense frames, overlapping strokes fuse into a flat grey mat and individual circles stop being readable as circles.
critique.action: Either clip nothing or clip everything on a declared margin. Set a hard 4-6% inset for all geometry so no arc is severed by the viewBox, or push the bleed hard enough (elements 1.5x frame) that it reads as intentional cropping. Trace and remove the two orphan horizontal segments in the 175 neutral path. Cap overdraw at the centre — enforce a minimum spacing so no more than about 4 strokes cross within any 8px radius, which kills both the starburst knot and the grey fusion.

critique.observation: These unambiguously read as one project. The hexagon-plus-ring-plus-scatter vocabulary and the single palette hold across all twelve seeds and all three states with no outlier. If anything this axis passes for the wrong reason: the coherence comes from the seeds being too similar rather than from a shared visual language expressed differently, so the fix demanded under seedVariation must be executed WITHOUT breaking this.
critique.action: When you add the structural seed axes, hold the invariants fixed as the identity carrier: same centre, same palette assignments by role, same tick geometry, same stroke-weight ratios. Vary counts and radii, never the grammar.

critique.observation: Holds. On states.png, seed 138 keeps its distinctive closed double ring through all three states, 212 keeps its hexagon-inscribed-in-circle, 101 keeps its hexagon-plus-three-lobe armature, and 175 keeps its dense six-fold halo. No seed becomes a different object under drawdown. Note the caveat this shares with thumbnailSurvival: same-seed continuity survives, but cross-seed distinctness does not survive into stress or recovery, so a viewer can tell that 212-stress is still 212 only by having 212-neutral beside it.
critique.action: Preserve this when you rework the states. Whatever the structural seed axes turn out to be, ring count and radius ratio must be seed-owned and state-invariant; let the state change only which arcs are drawn and how far out they extend, never the armature the seed chose.

critique.observation: GATE FAIL, but a much narrower one than before. The ink flood is gone and some of these frames are handsome. Three things still stop it reading as an orrery. FIRST, nothing is graduated. Across all 36 frames on contact.png and states.png there is not one tick, not one index mark, not one numeral ring, no pointer, no gnomon, no vernier. The closest thing is the irregular dash gaps in the cream rings of 138, 212 and 508 — I count 2 to 4 uneven gaps per ring, which reads as a broken stroke, not as a graduation ladder. Nothing here was built to measure. SECOND, the dominant relation between elements is tangency and offset, not nesting. 360, 397 and 471 neutral are a brass circle and a teal circle of near-equal radius offset by roughly 10% of that radius, which reads as a double-printed misregistration; 101, 323 and 434 neutral put a brass hexagon and a teal circle at the same size crossing at four points; 138 and 508 are flower-of-life rosettes of same-radius cream circles, tangent side by side. In 286 neutral the four rings step down in radius but each is shifted upward so they touch at 12 o'clock — hoops on a nail, not concentric. True shared-centre nests appear in only 3 of 36 frames: 212's hexagon-in-hexagon-in-hexagon core, and 175 stress's brass ring around a teal ring. THIRD, it is not engraved. Every stroke is uniform width, soft, opaque and round-capped; the bearing dots in 175 carry soft drop shadows. There is no hairline-against-heavy contrast anywhere in a single ring stack.
critique.action: Take the armature of 175 stress — the one frame that is genuinely an instrument — and make it the template. Replace the tangent-child recursion with 5 rings on ONE shared centre at radii 0.30 / 0.45 / 0.62 / 0.78 / 0.90 of the frame half-width, alternating stroke weight 0.75px hairline and 2.5px heavy so the ratio is at least 3:1. Graduate the 0.62 and 0.90 rings with 72 radial ticks each, ticks 5px long drawn perpendicular to the ring, every sixth tick doubled to 10px and drawn in brass. Add one pointer per token: a single straight brass spoke from centre to the 0.90 ring, terminating in a filled triangle 8px wide. Retire the flower-of-life layout in 138 and 508 entirely; it is mandala grammar, not instrument grammar. Delete the near-equal-radius offset pair in 360, 397 and 471 — force any second primary circle to be at most 0.7x or at least 1.4x the first, never within 15% of it.

critique.observation: The state change is now one clean scalar and it is unmistakable at 120px: the teal orbit's radius. On states.png seed 101 the teal circle sits inside the hexagon in stress, circumscribes it in neutral, and swallows it in recovery, while the brass hexagon and the right-hand satellite chain never move. Seed 212 and 175 do the same. Half the brief is delivered: recovery genuinely opens wider. The other half runs backwards, exactly as it did in round 1. Drawdown is supposed to cut generations away so the instrument reads as incomplete, and nothing in the stress row is incomplete. In 175 stress the brass ring is a closed, unbroken circle, the teal ring inside it is closed and unbroken, and all six cream bearings are present and whole — it is the cleanest, most resolved, most instrument-like frame in the entire packet, and it is the wounded state. No arc is severed, no ring is dropped leaving an empty radius, no tick ladder is truncated, in any of the twelve stress frames. Recovery also fails the 'more rings' half: 101, 175 and 212 have exactly the same element count in all three states — only the radius moved.
critique.action: Stop animating radius and start animating which arcs exist. For stress: erase 35-50% of each ring's circumference in 2-3 gaps of 40-70 degrees so rings render as open segments with visible ends, delete 2 of the 5 concentric rings outright and leave their radii empty so the gap in the stack is readable, and cut the graduated tick ladder off mid-run at a random bearing so it stops halfway around. Hold the outer ring radius CONSTANT under stress so the wound is a hole in something whole, not a smaller tidy object. For recovery: keep the neutral rings where they are, forbid any new mark inside the neutral inner radius, and ADD 3 rings at 1.15x, 1.35x and 1.55x the neutral outer radius so the count genuinely rises from 5 to 8 and the instrument grows past its own bounds.

critique.observation: Real movement since round 1, and it is visible: on contact-thumb.png the teal now separates cleanly from the brown ground in 101, 175, 249, 286, 323, 360, 434 and 471, so the palette is four colours at browse size instead of two. The neutral row of states-thumb.png resolves to about six looks instead of three. But two of the three rows still collapse. In the stress row, 101, 323 and 434 are the identical stamp — brass hexagon with one small teal circle inside it — and 360, 397 and 471 are three near-empty dark frames with a small pale cluster below centre that cannot be told apart. In the recovery row, 101, 323 and 434 are again one look, and 249, 360, 397 and 471 are all 'two big pale circles overlapping'. 138 and 508 are one look in every row. So in stress and recovery, seven of twelve seeds are confusable at 120px. The other problem the thumb sheet exposes: seven of twelve neutrals carry the same bilateral tic — one pale bead at 9 o'clock and one at 3 o'clock, both at exact mid-height (101, 249, 286, 323, 360, 397, 434, 471). At 120px that horizontal bar-bell silhouette is the strongest shape signal on the sheet and it is shared, so it actively erases the differences underneath it.
critique.action: Break the bar-bell: place each seed's satellite dial at a seed-chosen clock angle drawn from 12 distinct positions 30 degrees apart, and forbid the 3-o'clock/9-o'clock pair entirely. Give each seed one silhouette decision that is state-invariant and survives at 120px — set concentric ring count per seed across 4 to 8 and outer radius across 0.55 to 0.92 of the frame half-width, and hold both fixed through stress and recovery. Raise the stress-state floor: no stress frame may occupy less than 55% of the frame's shorter dimension, which pulls 360, 397 and 471 stress back off the empty-frame reading. Target to test on states-thumb.png: any two of the twelve STRESS frames distinguishable side by side at 120px, which is currently false for 101/323/434 and for 360/397/471.

critique.observation: Genuine progress. This is no longer one recipe at twelve densities — I can name about five families on contact.png: hexagon-crossing-circle (101, 323, 434), flower-of-life rosette (138, 508), beaded orbit (175, 212), offset circle pair with side beads (360, 397, 471, and 249 with a hexagon added), and the descending ring stack (286). Structural things now vary: the hexagon is present or absent, the rosette count is 0, 6 or 12, a nested inner polygon appears in 212 and 323, and 286 has a four-deep stack nobody else has. But twelve seeds resolving to five families means three near-duplicate groups, and the duplicates are close: 101, 323 and 434 differ only in whether there is a tiny hexagon at centre and how bright the side beads are; 360 and 471 differ only in which way the brass circle is offset; 138 and 508 differ only by the shape of the dark knot at the centre, which is illegible anyway.
critique.action: Add a third and fourth independent structural axis so the families stop clustering. Vary the inscribed polygon across four values — triangle, square, hexagon, none — instead of hexagon-or-nothing, so 101, 323 and 434 cannot land on the same one. Vary the inner-to-outer radius ratio across 0.20 to 0.60 in steps, so 360 and 471 separate by proportion rather than by offset direction. Make the satellite dial present in only about 60% of seeds instead of nearly all of them. Cap any family at 2 of 12 seeds: the offset-circle-pair family currently holds 4, which is a third of the collection on one idea.

critique.observation: Improved from an even field of incident to something with rest and a subject: 175 neutral, 175 stress and 286 neutral all have one dominant ring and a large quiet centre, and the ink cut is the single biggest gain in this round. Two problems remain. Frame occupancy still swings roughly 2:1 across neighbours on the same sheet — 286 neutral and 397 neutral sit at about 55% of frame height with wide dead margins, while 508 and 138 neutral bleed off all four edges.
