critique.observation: There is a shared substrate - the same cold blue-slate bed vocabulary and the same white stroke material appear in every frame - so these are not strangers. But 397 (pure horizontal bedding, no white) and 360 (a white fan on an almost bare ground) sit at opposite ends of a range wide enough that a browser meeting only those two would not place them in the same project.
critique.action: Once the white layer is capped and the bedding carries the variance, both outliers move toward the middle on their own. Verify by putting 360, 397 and 138 side by side at 120px; they should share a silhouette family and differ in bedding rhythm.

critique.observation: The white starburst knot is gone and every frame is now horizontal bedding in cold blue-slate, which is real progress on the subject. But the brief's explicit prohibition survives in the majority of the set: 175, 249, 286, 360, 434 and 471 are stacks whose beds are all centred on the vertical midline, tapering from wide slabs at top and bottom to a pinched pale waist at mid-frame, with dark empty margins of roughly 60-110px on BOTH sides at 512px. Seed 175 neutral is a near-perfect mirror about x=256 - it reads as a totem or a stacked pedestal, not a core. 360 is a floating stack of grey plates dead-centre with margin on all four sides. Only 101, 138, 323, 397 and 508 read as the wide, edge-to-edge core the brief asks for.
critique.action: Kill the centring rule for good: draw each bed from an independently sampled left edge in 0.00-0.45 and right edge in 0.55-1.00 of frame width instead of a width centred on 0.5, and require at least 8 of every 12 beds to terminate ON a frame edge (left or right) so no vertical mirror axis can form. Reject-and-resample any frame whose bed-centre x values have a standard deviation below 12% of frame width. Target the 397 and 508 read as the collection default and the 175/360/471 read as impossible, not rare.

critique.observation: The brief's second market clause - 'recovery should rule bright lines through the whole field' - is not delivered. In 138, 175 and 212 recovery is the neutral frame plus four to six short pale segments confined to the middle third, spanning roughly x=160-360 of 512 and stopping well short of both edges. Nothing rules through the whole field. On the 120px states sheet, the recovery row and the neutral row are indistinguishable for 175, 397, 434, 471 and 508.
critique.action: Replace the recovery seams with 4-6 full-bleed rules that start at x=0 and end at x=512 (bleed 4% past both edges), distributed over the full frame height rather than the middle third, at a slope within +/-2 degrees. Raise their luminance to roughly 1.8-2.2x the local ground so a rule crossing the dark upper field stays visible, and verify the change is nameable at 120px before shipping it.

critique.observation: There is a focal hierarchy, and in the centred family it is pointed at the wrong thing: a pale ash lens sitting at the exact middle of the frame is the brightest and largest object in 212, 249, 286, 434 and 471, so the eye lands on a blob at mid-height instead of travelling top-down through the sequence. Above and below it the frame is unused - 249 has empty dark ground across the top 12% and bottom 12%, 434 across the top 8% and bottom 5%. In 286 and 249 the lowest bed sits below a clear gap and reads as a detached element rather than the deepest bed.
critique.action: Push bedding to fill 96% of frame height with no gap over 3% of height anywhere in the stack, and remove the gap above the lowest bed so the sequence is continuous to the bottom edge. Redistribute the pale ash so no more than 25% of its total ink falls in the middle third of frame height; scatter the remainder across the top and bottom thirds so the brightest seam is as likely to be the second bed from the top as the seventh.

critique.observation: The blues are genuinely a family - glacial blue, slate and wet shale sit in a tight value band and hold across all twelve seeds - and the near-white planks from before are gone. Two problems remain. The ash is no longer thin in 101 and 360: in 101 the two largest slabs (top and bottom) are mid-grey ash and blue survives only as a small accent in the middle, and 360 is essentially an all-ash frame with two blue beds. And the ground still lightens as it descends - sampled on 175 neutral it runs (10,16,22) at the top edge to (22,35,43) at the bottom, a 2x luminance rise downward, which inverts the depth logic of a core read from the top down.
critique.action: Cap total ash coverage at 15% of frame area per seed and forbid ash on the single largest bed of any frame, so it stays a seam rather than the ground mass; 101 and 360 should lose roughly two thirds of their current grey. Flip the background ramp so the bottom is the dark end - (22,35,43) at the top to (10,16,22) at the bottom - or flatten it to a uniform (14,22,29) and let the beds carry all the depth.

critique.observation: The bimodal split from before is gone - nothing is a fan any more, and every seed is legible stratigraphy - but the middle cluster has only shrunk, not dissolved. On the 120px contact sheet 212, 249, 286 and 434 are one repeated icon: blue stripes tapering to a pale centre with dark side margins. 397 and 508 are a second pair (bright, full-bleed, dense); 101 and 360 a third (pale grey, ash-dominant). That is roughly five silhouette families across twelve seeds.
critique.action: Make bed rhythm, not bed brightness, the seed differentiator: vary bed count across seeds over at least a 3x range (6 to 20 beds) and individual bed thickness over a 5x range within each frame, and give each seed one of four mass profiles - top-heavy, bottom-heavy, evenly laminated, or two thick slabs with fine laminae between. Assign 212, 249, 286 and 434 four different profiles and re-check that no two of the twelve share a silhouette at 120px.

critique.observation: At 120px the horizontal banding survives cleanly and the blue family holds together, which is the win. What does not survive is identity within the centred cluster - 212, 249, 286 and 434 collapse to the same striped-with-a-grey-waist icon - and 323 goes murky, its beds sitting so close in value against the dark ground that it reads as a single dark smear rather than a stack.
critique.action: Enforce a minimum value separation of about 12 sRGB steps between vertically adjacent beds so no two neighbours merge at 120px, which will lift 323 out of the smear. Then verify the twelve neutral thumbs at 120px only, and reject the sheet if any two frames share both a mass profile and an edge profile.

critique.observation: Drawdown is delivered and it is unmistakable at browse size, which is the strongest result on the sheet. Compare 138 neutral to 138 stress: the count roughly doubles from about 11 beds to about 18, the empty gaps at mid-frame fill in, and the new beds run wider and touch both edges. 212, 249, 323 and 471 all show the same at 120px. Recovery is the weak half - 175 recovery differs from 175 neutral by a handful of pale hairlines in the middle third and nothing else, and at 120px most recovery frames are their own neutral frame.
critique.action: Keep the stress behaviour exactly as it is. For recovery, add the full-bleed bright rules described above AND drop bed count by roughly 25% from the neutral baseline so the field visibly opens as the rules go in - two changes rather than one, so the recovery frame differs from neutral in both count and mark type and can be told apart at 120px.

critique.observation: Holds, and it holds better than last round. 175 keeps its two top slabs, its two bottom slabs and its bed positions across all three states; 138 keeps its thick teal band at upper-mid and its isolated blue bar near the bottom; 212 keeps its top pair and its wide bottom bar even though stress strips the pale centre out. Same seed, three states, obviously the same object each time.
critique.action: Preserve this when you add the recovery rules: anchor the largest three beds of each seed by position and thickness so they are byte-identical across neutral, stress and recovery, and let only the thin laminae and the ash seams move. Do not let the 25% recovery bed reduction remove any of those three anchors.

critique.observation: Four named and located. Collision mush: in 286 the middle third is six pale beds of near-identical value stacked with no dark separator, fusing into one undifferentiated wedge where individual beds are no longer separable; 212 neutral has the same at its centre. Foreign shape: 249 neutral carries a bright blue block at about 27% across and 65% down that is roughly as tall as it is wide, breaking the horizontal-only vocabulary of every other mark and reading as a rendering error. Vanishing strokes: the hairline rules across the upper third of 471 and 175 sit within a few sRGB steps of the ground and disappear at 120px. Detached bed: the lowest bar in 286 and 249 sits under a clear gap and reads as a UI element rather than the base of the core.
critique.action: Insert a 1-2px ground-coloured separator between any two adjacent beds whose luminance differs by less than 12 steps, which resolves 286 and 212. Clamp every drawn rectangle to an aspect ratio of at least 4:1 wide so the 249 block cannot occur. Floor stroke luminance at 1.8x the local ground so upper-field hairlines on 471 and 175 lift. Remove the vertical gap above the lowest bed in every seed.

critique.observation: These are members of one project. Every frame speaks the same vocabulary - hard-edged horizontal rectangles of varying thickness, a cold blue-slate family, pale ash seams, a near-black ground - and the round-1 outliers are gone: nothing has abandoned the strata. 360 stretches the family furthest by being almost entirely grey, and 101 leans the same way, but both still place inside the project.
critique.action: Hold this. When ash is capped at 15% per the palette note, re-check 360, 101 and 397 side by side at 120px; they should share the blue-dominant ground and differ only in bedding rhythm and mass profile.

critique.observation: The brief asks for a wide silhouette with no centred emblem. All twelve neutral frames are still a mirror-symmetric stack of bars floating inside dark margins on BOTH sides — the same finding as rounds 1 and 2, visibly unacted on. On the contact sheet no bed in eleven of the twelve seeds touches a left or right frame edge (286 manages 2% of its rows); median dark margin runs 32-64px per side on a 256px cell, i.e. roughly a fifth of the frame width is empty ground on each flank. Bed centres cluster on the midline: their standard deviation is 0.9% of frame width in 360, 1.4% in 175, and never exceeds 5.6% (101) anywhere in the set. 138 is a literal hourglass — pale slabs widest at the upper and lower thirds pinching to a waist at mid-height, symmetric about x=128. 101, 249 and 471 each put their brightest pale lens at dead centre. The thing a viewer names is a totem or a stacked pedestal on a card, not a drill core laid horizontally that runs off both edges. 397 is the one frame that reads as the brief.
critique.action: Replace the centred-width sampler with independent per-bed edges: sample each bed's left edge in 0.00-0.40 and its right edge in 0.60-1.00 of frame width, and force at least 8 of every 12 beds to terminate ON a frame edge with a 4% bleed past it. Reject and resample any frame whose bed-centre x standard deviation falls under 12% of frame width — every one of the twelve currently measures between 0.9% and 5.6%. Make 397's edge-to-edge read the collection default and 360's 41px-per-side margin unreachable.

critique.observation: The brief's second market clause — recovery should rule bright lines through the whole field — is now half delivered. Round 2's complaint that the recovery seams were confined to the middle third is genuinely fixed: 175 recovery carries about eleven pale rules spread from y=50 to y=490 of 512. But nothing rules through the WHOLE field, because the rules stop short of both edges — the widest rule in 175 recovery leaves 30px of dark ground at the left and 42px at the right. And in the two dense seeds recovery is barely a state at all: at 120px the mean-luminance difference between neutral and recovery is 7.5 for 508 and 9.9 for 397, against 22.6 for 175 and 34.3 for 323.
critique.action: Extend every recovery rule to full bleed — draw from x=-20 to x=532 on a 512 frame — and guarantee a minimum of 4 such rules per seed in every state where recovery applies. For 397 and 508 specifically, pair the rules with a 25% cut in bed count relative to their neutral baseline, so recovery differs from neutral in mark COUNT as well as mark TYPE and can be named at 120px.

critique.observation: There is a focal hierarchy and in half the set it lands on a bright mass at the exact centre of the frame: the pale cluster in 101 sits at mid-height and mid-width, as does 249's, 471's and 138's waist. The frame is also under-used. Measured on the contact cells, 360 inks only 156 of 256 rows (61%) with 34px of dead ground across the top; 101 inks 65% with 23px dead at the top; 212 and 175 leave 26-28px. 397 inks 238 rows (93%) with no internal gap over 6px, which proves the runtime can fill a frame and simply is not asked to.
critique.action: Push bedding to 397's 93% of frame height in every seed and cap any internal gap at 3% of height; 360, 212, 175, 249 and 101 each need their 23-34px of top dead ground closed. Redistribute the pale ash so no more than 25% of its total ink falls in the middle third of frame height, so the brightest seam is as likely to be the second bed from the top as the seventh.

critique.observation: These are one project. Every frame speaks the same vocabulary — hard-edged horizontal rectangles of varying thickness, cold blue-slate, pale ash seams, near-black ground — and round 1's off-project outliers (the white fans, the blade tangles) are entirely gone. The family stretches furthest at two ends: 323 is desaturated to a mean of 0.25 with 16.5% of its area above luminance 110, so it reads as a grey high-key frame beside 397's 0.45 saturation; and 360 is nearly ashless at 1.5% and very dark. Both still place inside the project.
critique.action: Pull the two ends in: raise 323's mean saturation from 0.25 into the 0.33-0.45 band the other ten occupy, and cut its ash coverage from 16.5% to under 10%. Lift 360's bed-to-ground luminance separation so that, placed beside 397 and 138 at 120px, all three share a blue-dominant ground and differ only in bedding rhythm.

critique.observation: Two named faults from earlier rounds are genuinely fixed and the palette is now the strongest non-market axis. The ground ramp is flipped as asked — sampled down the left margin of 175 neutral it runs (22,35,43) at the top to (10,16,22) at the bottom, so the frame now darkens as it descends and the ground supports the top-down core read instead of fighting it. The ash is a seam again: peak luminance across the set is 175-192 with no pixel above 200, and area above luminance 140 is only 1.3-4.3% in nine of twelve seeds. What remains is that ash has migrated onto the largest beds of two frames: 323's two top slabs and two bottom slabs are near-white planks (16.5% of area above 110, 12.8% above 140) and 138 runs 14.4%/9.5%, so in those two the ash is the ground mass rather than the seam.
critique.action: Cap ash at 10% of frame area per seed and forbid it on the two largest beds of any frame; 323 and 138 each need roughly a third of their grey ink converted to slate or wet shale, leaving near-white only for seams under 4px thick.

critique.observation: The range is wider than round 2 — 397 (dense, 93% coverage) against 360 (61%, 1.5% ash) against 323 (high-key grey slabs) against 175 and 434 (sparse hairline ladders) is real spread. But 101, 249, 471 and 286 are still one icon: dark ground, 46-61px margins per side, blue stripes, a pale cluster near mid-height, and a detached bar at the bottom. And the spread that exists is carried by density and brightness rather than by shape — total inked rows run only 156 to 238 across the twelve, a 1.5x range, so every frame has the same silhouette and differs in fill.
critique.action: Assign 101, 249, 471 and 286 four different mass profiles — top-heavy, bottom-heavy, evenly laminated, and two thick slabs with fine laminae between — and widen bed count across seeds to at least a 3x range from the present 1.5x. Make bedding rhythm the seed differentiator and demote ash brightness to a secondary variable.

critique.observation: At 120px the horizontal banding survives cleanly and the blue family holds, which is the win. Counting distinct icons on the neutral thumb row I get about six across twelve: 138 (hourglass), 212 (white blob), 323 (bright slabs top and bottom), 397 (dense blue block), 175 and 434 (near-twin sparse hairline ladders), 508 (dense, varied), and then 101/249/471/286 collapsing into one striped-with-a-pale-waist stamp. 360 does not survive at all — its beds sit within a few sRGB steps of the ground and at 120px it is a dark rectangle with two white scratches, which is round 2's 323-murk finding relocated rather than closed.
critique.action: Enforce a minimum 12 sRGB steps of luminance between vertically adjacent beds AND between every bed and its local ground, which lifts 360 out of the smear. Then split the 175/434 twins by giving one of them 3 dominant thick beds and the other 18 fine laminations, and verify the sheet at 120px only, rejecting it if any two of the twelve share both a mass profile and an edge profile.

critique.observation: Both directions are now visible at browse size, which is the headline improvement of this round. Drawdown is unmistakable: 175 goes from 40.3% to 59.3% ink coverage under stress, its median side margin closes from 110px to 74px, its top ink row rises from y=52 to y=14, and its bright marks fall away — across the whole stress row bright coverage drops in every seed (101 from 4.9% to 1.0%, 249 from 9.0% to 4.0%), so the stress row reads at 120px as the dense quiet row. Recovery, which was the failure last round, now reads too: it spreads eleven bright rules over the full height of 175 and lifts bright coverage from 5.6% to 8.9%. The residue is three seeds — 508 and 397, whose recovery is nearly their own neutral at 120px, and 360, whose stress and recovery differ by a mean luminance of only 4.7.
critique.action: Keep the stress behaviour exactly as it is. Repair the three weak recovery cases only: give 508, 397 and 360 at least 4 full-bleed bright rules each and drop their recovery bed count 25% below their neutral baseline, so the field visibly opens as the rules go in.

critique.observation: Holds across all four seeds on the states sheet. 175 keeps its dark top slab, its thick band at about two thirds down and its overall bed skeleton through neutral, stress and recovery; 138 keeps its hourglass in all three; 212 keeps its centre blob and its wide bottom slab; 101 keeps its bed positions. Same seed, three states, obviously the same object each time. The weakest case is 101, where stress strips the pale focal cluster from 4.9% to 1.0% bright coverage and the frame loses the element the eye was landing on, though the bar positions still identify it.
critique.action: Preserve this when the 25% recovery bed reduction goes in: anchor the three thickest beds of each seed by position and thickness so they are identical across neutral, stress and recovery, and let only the thin laminae and ash seams move. Hold 101's stress reduction as a ratio rather than an absolute so it keeps at least a third of its pale cluster.

critique.observation: Four, named and located. (1) 212, in all three states: an irregular non-rectangular white cloud at frame centre, about x=100-175 and y=145-195 of 256, with stepped diagonal edges — the only non-horizontal mark in the collection, the brightest object in its frame, and it reads as a smear or a render fault. (2) 138, upper middle: six adjacent pale beds with no dark separator fusing into one undifferentiated grey wedge from about y=105 to y=200, where individual beds are no longer separable — round 2's collision mush, moved from 286 to 138. (3) Detached lowest bed under a clear gap of 13-21px (5-8% of frame height) in 101, 138, 175, 286 and 434; on the 512px single of 175 neutral that gap measures 41px and the bottom rule reads as a UI element rather than the deepest bed. This one was named in round 1 and again in round 2 and is unchanged. (4) The inverse of round 1's clipping problem: nothing bleeds off the frame anywhere, every mark terminating 5-41px inside the viewBox, so each token reads as an object printed on a card rather than a section cut through ground.
critique.action: Clamp every drawn mark to a rectangle of aspect ratio 4:1 or wider so 212's centre cloud cannot form. Insert a 2px ground-coloured separator between any two adjacent beds whose luminance differs by less than 12 steps, which dissolves the fused wedge at y=105-200 in 138. Delete the 13-21px gap above the lowest bed in 101, 138, 175, 286 and 434 so the sequence runs continuous to the bottom edge. And bleed the outermost beds 4% past the left and right frame boundary rather than insetting them.

critique.observation: The subject is gone. Across all twelve neutral cells on the contact sheet there is not one stack of horizontal sediment bands anywhere. The substrate is 8-15 translucent blue squares, each rotated roughly 5-20 degrees off axis and each about as tall as it is wide (clearest in 101, 249, 471 and 508), so it reads as scattered panes of glass rather than as bedding. The drawing on top is long pale bars at every angle including near-vertical: 175 neutral is a crossed thicket in which the two steepest strokes run within about 5 degrees of vertical, 434 neutral is a diagonal fan sweeping from the lower left, 286 neutral is six long diagonals. The word a viewer reaches for looking at this sheet is shattered, or pick-up sticks. It is not drill core. Whatever horizontal bedding existed before is absent from every frame in this packet.
critique.action: Replace the rotated-square substrate with axis-aligned rectangles: height 2-12% of frame height, width 100% of frame width, rotation removed from the parameter set entirely so no substrate mark can tilt. Stack 8-20 of them top to bottom per seed with no vertical gap over 3% of height. Make 397's horizontal bar cluster the collection default and make 434's diagonal fan unreachable.

critique.observation: The brief's two explicit prohibitions - no radial symmetry, no centred emblem - are now the dominant motif rather than an occasional lapse. 138 neutral and 138 recovery are literal starbursts: twenty to thirty pale blades radiating from a single interior point at roughly x=140, y=205 of the 256px cell, the recovery cell reading as a sea urchin. 212 neutral, 249 neutral, 471 neutral and 101 neutral each carry a convergence knot at mid-frame. 175 neutral has a visible bright node dot where six strokes meet at about x=440, y=258 of 512. This is the same finding logged in rounds 1, 2 and 3, and the pictures are further from the brief on it now than they were in round 1.
critique.action: Delete the shared-origin sampler that gives strokes a common anchor. Give every bar an independently sampled y in 0.02-0.98 of frame height and cap slope at plus or minus 3 degrees from horizontal, then reject-and-resample any frame in which more than 2 bars pass within 8px of a common point. Verify on 138 and 212 specifically that no interior convergence node survives.

critique.observation: The brief says drawdown should lay down MORE beds. The states sheet delivers the opposite, and delivers it unmistakably. On the 120px states sheet the stress row is the EMPTY row in all twelve columns: 175 stress keeps two full-width rules and three near-vertical strokes against roughly twenty marks in its neutral, 434 stress is three faint lines on bare blue, 508 stress is a single small X in an otherwise empty cell, 212 stress drops to four bars. The transition is legible at browse size, which is the good news, and it is backwards.
critique.action: Invert the stress mapping: raise bed count under drawdown by at least 60% above the neutral baseline (12 beds becomes 20) and place the added beds as thin full-width laminae in the currently empty upper and lower thirds, so the stress cell of 175, 434 and 508 is the densest of its three states rather than the sparsest.

critique.observation: The recovery clause - rule bright lines through the whole field - is delivered in only three of twelve. 175, 286 and 323 recovery genuinely cross the frame. In 101, 138, 212 and 508 recovery the added bright bars are short, pile into the same centre knot, and stop 40-90px short of both edges on a 256px cell, so nothing rules through anything. Worse, the two genuinely full-width rules in seed 175 sit at the top and bottom edge in ALL THREE states - they are present identically in 175 neutral, 175 stress and 175 recovery - so the one element that does span the field carries no recovery signal at all.
critique.action: Draw every recovery rule from x=-20 to x=532 on a 512 frame, minimum 4 per seed, distributed over the full frame height rather than the middle band. Remove the two always-on full-width rules from 175's neutral and stress states so that their appearance becomes the recovery tell instead of a constant.

critique.observation: The work floats in the middle of the frame and the eye lands on the forbidden thing. 101 leaves its bottom-right quadrant as bare dark ground, 138 leaves a dark band down the right fifth of the cell plus bare ground at top-left, 212 leaves both the top-left and bottom-right corners empty, 508 leaves the right third of the cell essentially unused, and 397 carries a solid near-black square in its lower-right that reads as a hole rather than as ground. In 101, 138, 212, 249 and 471 the brightest and largest object is the white knot at mid-frame, so the eye stops there instead of travelling top-down through a sequence.
critique.action: Extend the substrate to 100% of frame width and at least 96% of frame height in every seed, closing the dark flanks in 101, 138, 212 and 508 and filling 397's black lower-right square. Cap any internal gap at 3% of frame height. Cut the pale bar layer's total ink by about 50% so the substrate, not the bars, is read first.

critique.observation: The cold family is genuinely chosen and it is the best thing here: glacial blue, slate and wet shale sit in a tight value band across all twelve seeds and the ground is a consistent near-black navy in every frame. Two faults. First, the pale ash is near-white and roughly 12-20px wide at 512 and is the largest and brightest object in every single frame (101, 138, 212, 249, 323, 471 most obviously), so the one element the brief called a thin seam is the subject of the picture. Second, the blue squares sit within a few steps of each other in value, so where they overlap - 175 stress, 360 neutral, 397 neutral - they fuse into one flat plate with no separable layers.
critique.action: Cut ash stroke width by about 65%, from 12-20px to 4-6px at 512, drop its peak luminance about 30% from near-white to a pale grey-blue, and cap total ash at 10% of frame area per seed. Then spread the blue substrate across at least 4 distinct value steps separated by 12 or more sRGB each, so the overlaps in 360 and 397 separate into readable layers.

critique.observation: On the 120px neutral row I count about four families across twelve frames: a centred white asterisk (101, 212, 249, 471, 508), a crossed-sticks thicket (175, 286, 323), a radiating spine (138), and a diagonal fan (434), with 360 and 397 as faint low-contrast variants of the first two. The spread that does exist is carried by density and brightness, not by shape - every frame has the same centred-blob silhouette with dark flanks, so these are one work at twelve densities rather than twelve works.
critique.action: Assign 101, 212, 249, 471 and 508 five different mass profiles - top-heavy, bottom-heavy, evenly laminated, two thick slabs with fine laminae between, and one dominant bed - and widen bed count across seeds to a 3x range, 6 to 20. Then re-check the twelve neutral thumbs at 120px only and reject the sheet if any two share both a mass profile and an edge profile.

critique.observation: At 120px the pale bars do survive and the blue family holds together, which is the win. What does not survive: 360 neutral does not read at all - its bars sit within a few sRGB steps of its own blue ground and the cell is a dull rectangle with three faint scratches; 434 stress and 508 stress are near-empty cells; and six of the twelve neutral thumbs are the same white-scribble-on-blue stamp. Nothing on either 120px sheet says sediment, core or time at browse size.
critique.action: Floor every bar at 12 sRGB steps above its local ground so 360's marks lift out of the smear, and set a minimum ink coverage of about 25% of cell area in every state so 508 stress and 434 stress cannot render as near-empty cells. Verify by viewing contact-thumb.png and states-thumb.png at 120px only.

critique.observation: Two of the four seeds on the states sheet hold and two do not. 101 keeps its horizontal bar grid and its blue square at lower-left through neutral, stress and recovery; 138 keeps its radiating spine and its detached square at top-left in all three. 212 does not survive: neutral is a starburst, stress is a legible capital E, recovery is a scribble knot - three different objects wearing the same blue background. 175 stress discards roughly 85% of its strokes and keeps only the two full-width rules and a centre pair, so the stress frame is nearly a different work.
critique.action: Anchor the three thickest bars of each seed by position and thickness so they render identically across neutral, stress and recovery, and express every state change as a ratio with a floor - never let any state fall below 40% of the neutral mark count, which is exactly what breaks 212 and 175 stress.

critique.observation: Five, named and located. (1) 212 stress: the pale bars resolve into a legible capital letter E at mid-frame, a glyph in a collection that contains no other glyph, and it is the brightest object in its cell. (2) 138, all three states: six to eight blue squares float detached in the left and right margins, separated from the main mass by bare dark ground, reading as stray UI chips rather than as part of the work. (3) 175 neutral: six strokes converge to a small bright node dot at about x=440, y=258 of 512, which is the brightest pixel in the frame and reads as a render fault. (4) Collision mush at the centre of 138 recovery, 323 neutral and 249 recovery, where overlapping blades fuse into an undifferentiated white pile in which individual strokes are no longer separable. (5) 397 neutral: a solid near-black square filling much of the lower-right quadrant that reads as a hole punched through the field. Separately, strokes terminate hard on all four frame edges throughout 175, 286 and 323, and 434's fan is sliced flat at the left edge so it reads as chopped.
critique.action: Clamp every drawn mark to an aspect ratio of 6:1 or wider so 212's E and its crossbars cannot form. Delete any substrate square whose nearest neighbour sits more than 8% of frame width away, which removes 138's floating chips. Cap overlapping bright strokes at 3 deep and drop per-stroke opacity to about 0.55 so the centre of 138 recovery stays readable as separate lines. Raise 397's black lower-right square to at least 12 sRGB steps above the ground or delete it. Bleed the outermost marks 4% past the left and right boundary instead of terminating them on it.

critique.observation: These are unmistakably members of one project. Every frame on the contact sheet is pale bars over translucent blue squares on a near-black navy ground, there are no strangers, and even the two extremes - 360's faint low-contrast cell and 323's dense white tangle - place inside the family. The coherence is if anything too tight: the family is held together by one repeated motif rather than by a shared vocabulary used differently, which is why the seedVariation axis fails at the same time this one passes.
critique.action: Keep the near-black navy ground and the blue family exactly as they are - they are the only part of the brief this packet delivers - and route all new variance into bedding rhythm per the seedVariation action rather than into new mark types, so that 138 and 397 remain siblings while ceasing to be the same picture.

critique.observation: The brief asks for dense horizontal scan-lines and the ghost of a raster. Almost nothing in this packet is horizontal. Every dense tile (212, 249, 286, 323, 508, and the seed-175 singles) is built from long DIAGONAL strokes radiating from a single centre point — the silhouette reads as a thistle, a burst, or a splayed handful of straws. Seed 397 is the only frame with any horizontal population at all, and even there the bands are crossed by diagonals of equal weight so no raster reads. There is no line register, no repeating row pitch, no dropout gaps punched through a continuous field, no rolling band. I did not see a screen carrying no picture; I saw a centred vector scribble on black. This is a wrong-primitive failure, not a wrong-parameter failure.
critique.action: Rebuild the base primitive. Replace the radial stroke emitter with a full-width horizontal band emitter: strokes spanning 100% of the viewBox width, y-positions quantised to a fixed row pitch of roughly 3-6px at 512 (so ~85-170 rows), stroke height 1-3px, near-zero rotation (cap any tilt at about ±1.5 degrees so it reads as a mistracking screen, not a fan). Get dropout from ROW ABSENCE and from horizontal segment breaks within a row — not from scattered floating squares. Keep the existing zigzag polylines only as a rare per-row displacement of the scan itself, never as free-floating confetti.

critique.observation: Every one of the twelve frames is a vertically-oriented blob parked in the centre with wide dead black margins left and right — in the seed-175 singles roughly the outer 25% of the frame on each side is empty, and in the 120px sheet the tiles read as a small object floating in a box. Within the blob there is no focal hierarchy either: the light-value zigzag cluster near the centre of 175 and the white cluster in 212 are the only candidates for a focus, and they are the same weight as the strokes crossing them, so the frame reads as an even field of incident inside an oval and empty outside it. The brief says the density IS the subject; a subject cannot be a centred object with margins.
critique.action: Fill the frame edge to edge. Extend the drawing to 100% of the viewBox on all four sides and delete the centre-biased placement entirely — for a scan-line field the correct distribution is uniform in y and full-bleed in x. Then build hierarchy from the raster itself rather than from a central cluster: one or two horizontal dropout BANDS of about 8-15% of frame height where rows go dark or shear, placed off-centre, as the only large-scale event in the frame.

critique.observation: There is a shared construction vocabulary — rotated rectangles, chunky zigzag polylines, long strokes, small scattered squares — and on the dense tiles you can see it is one generator. But the sheet does not hold together as one project, for two reasons visible side by side: seeds 138, 360, 471 and 434 carry essentially none of that vocabulary (they are black or near-black), and seed 397 uses an orthogonal band motif that appears nowhere else. So the contact sheet reads as one dense family, one blank family, and one outlier.
critique.action: Once the raster primitive lands, enforce a floor and a ceiling on the drawn ink so every seed is a member: require every frame to cover at least ~35% and at most ~80% of the canvas with lit rows. Retire the free-floating small-square population entirely, or demote it to at most 5-8 marks per frame sitting ON a scan row rather than in open black, so the same vocabulary appears in all twelve.

critique.observation: The brief specifies phosphor green and warm white on near-black with a THIN magenta chroma error. In three of twelve frames magenta is the dominant colour of the work — 101 and 323 are almost entirely hot pink with green relegated to a dark backing shape, and 508 is a pink slab crossed by green. In 286 the frame is white and grey with no green in it at all. So two of the three named roles are inverted somewhere in the collection. The near-black ground is the one part that works: it sits back and does not compete. The green itself is good — the bright mint in 212/249 does read as phosphor.
critique.action: Cap the chroma error by area, not by chance. Hold magenta to at most 3-5% of lit pixels in any frame, and restrict it to a fringe role: a 1-2px magenta offset copy of a green row, drawn only on rows that are already lit, never as a standalone stroke and never as its own scatter population. Guarantee green as the majority hue in every seed (target 60-80% of lit area), warm white as the highlight (10-25%), and remove the all-white variant (286) from the reachable space.

critique.observation: This fails in both directions at once, which is the worst case. Too narrow: 212, 249, 286, 323 and 508 are the same vertical starburst silhouette recoloured green, white and pink — at 120px I could not tell them apart by form, only by hue. Too wide: 138, 360 and 471 are empty black tiles, 434 is a faint wisp, and 397 is a different motif altogether. So the collection is simultaneously one work at five recolourings and five works that do not belong to it.
critique.action: Move the variation from HUE into STRUCTURE. Fix the palette per the axis above so colour stops carrying the differentiation, then vary the things a raster can vary: row pitch (3-8px), dropout band count (0-4) and their vertical placement, horizontal shear magnitude, chroma-offset distance, and the ratio of solid rows to broken rows. Target: a viewer at 120px can name which seed is which from silhouette alone with the hue removed. Simultaneously delete the empty region of the parameter space — see the thumbnail action.

critique.observation: This is where the packet fails hardest, and it fails on the sheet the round is decided on. On contact-thumb and states-thumb at 120px, seeds 138, 360 and 471 are indistinguishable from empty black rectangles in all three states — I could not see that anything had been drawn — and 434 is a few grey hairlines that vanish. That is four of twelve tokens, a third of the collection, rendering as nothing at browse size. Of the eight that do survive, five (212, 249, 286, 323, 508) collapse to the same spiky-ball stamp, so the sheet reads as roughly three distinct things plus four holes.
critique.action: Add a hard minimum-ink floor and raise the low end of every opacity and scale range. Concretely: require at least ~35% canvas coverage of lit rows per frame before a render is accepted, raise the minimum stroke alpha off the near-invisible dark-green values seen in 138/360/471 to no less than about 0.35 against the near-black ground, and remove whatever parameter combination produces the sparse-scatter mode entirely — it is not a quiet member of the collection, it is a blank. Re-render the 120px sheet and require twelve visibly distinct, visibly non-empty tiles before anything else is tuned.

critique.observation: The brief says volatility should TEAR THE RASTER APART and recovery should let the lines RE-LOCK. What actually changes between neutral and stress is that solid filled shapes thin into hairline outlines — in seed 175 the white blocks become thin white zigzag strokes, in 212 some of the white bulk drops out, in 101 a few strokes go thin. At 512 that is noticeable. On states-thumb at 120px it is invisible in ten of twelve seeds: 138, 360, 471 and 434 are blank in every state, and 101, 249, 286, 323, 397 and 508 look the same across the row. A state transition that cannot be seen at browse size has not been delivered. Recovery is faithful but there is nothing to recover FROM.
critique.action: Make stress a STRUCTURAL event, not a weight change. Under volatility, shear whole horizontal bands sideways by 10-30% of frame width, break rows into fragments (drop 30-50% of each row's length), collapse the row pitch irregularly, and push the magenta chroma offset from ~1px to ~8-12px so the colour fringe visibly separates. Under recovery, return pitch to uniform, restore row continuity to near-100%, and pull the chroma offset back to ~1px. Test by looking only at the 120px states sheet: the stress column must be identifiable without reading the captions.

critique.observation: This axis is the one thing that holds. Reading the states sheet row by row, each seed is unmistakably the same object across neutral, stress and recovery — 101 keeps its pink core and dark green backing shape, 175 keeps its exact dark-green cruciform and the position of its bright green squares top-right, 212 keeps its stroke layout and only sheds white. Recovery returns very close to neutral rather than to some third form. Nothing is replaced by a different work under drawdown.
critique.action: Preserve this when you rebuild. Whatever new stress deformation you add for the market-response axis, keep the seed-determined row placement and hue assignment fixed across all three states so the identity survives the much larger transition the brief actually asks for — deform the raster, do not reseed it.

critique.observation: Named and located: (1) in 397 a row of bright green squares is pinned along the extreme top edge and another along the extreme bottom edge, several of them cut in half by the viewBox — it reads as a border bug, not a decision; (2) in 508 and 471 there are isolated single small squares in the extreme corners of the frame, far from any other mark, which read as dead pixels rather than dropout; (3) in 212, 249, 286 and 508 the long diagonal strokes terminate hard against the frame edge while the composition floats away from it, so the cuts read as accidental rather than as bleed; (4) in the seed-175 neutral and recovery singles the pale zigzags and rotated squares near the centre overlap into an undifferentiated grey mush about 60px across where no individual shape is legible.
critique.action: Clip deliberately or not at all: once the drawing is full-bleed the edge cuts stop reading as errors. Remove the corner-scatter population that produces the isolated specks, and remove the top/bottom-edge square band in the 397 mode. For the centre mush, either reduce the overlapping pale element count by about half in that region or drop their fill opacity to ~0.4 and give them a 1px darker outline so individual shapes stay separable when stacked.

critique.observation: The primitive is now horizontal — that is real and it is the biggest change in the packet. But the brief asks for DENSE scan-lines and the ghost of a raster, and what I count in every tile of contact.png is roughly 20-30 chunky slabs of wildly varying height (in 138 a single pink block is about 100px tall at 512, taller than a third of the tiles' whole drawn stack). There is no row pitch. Nothing repeats at a fixed interval, so no raster is implied — the frames read as a hot-pink horizontal stripe painting or a datamoshed JPEG, not as a screen carrying no picture. The brief's 'density is the subject' is not delivered: the subject is the pink slab.
critique.action: Quantise every bar's y-position to a fixed per-seed row pitch of 3-6px at 512 (so 85-170 rows) and cap bar height at 1-4px, then build the big shapes by GROUPING adjacent rows of the same hue rather than by drawing one tall filled rectangle. No single filled block may exceed about 8px of height; a 100px pink mass must become ~20 lit rows at the same pitch as everything else.

critique.observation: The stated hierarchy is inverted. Magenta is the dominant hue in 11 of 12 tiles on contact.png — a saturated hot-pink filled slab is the largest and brightest object in 101, 138, 212, 249, 286, 323, 360, 397, 434, 471 and 508, and it is what your eye lands on first at 120px. A dark wine/maroon that appears nowhere in the brief is a second major mass (138 bottom, 286 top and bottom, 360 top and bottom, 434 middle, 101 stress). Phosphor green survives only as thin bright horizontal lines and is a clear minority in every tile and effectively absent from 175, 286, 323 and 471. The whites read cool grey-white, not warm. The near-black ground is the one part that is right — it sits back and does not compete.
critique.action: Hold magenta to at most 5% of lit pixels per frame and restrict it to a 1-3px offset fringe drawn only on rows that are already lit — delete the standalone filled magenta rectangle from the reachable space entirely. Delete the dark wine/maroon fill from the palette; it is a fourth colour the brief does not name. Raise phosphor green to 60-80% of lit area in every seed and warm the whites (shift the white toward roughly #F2EDE0) so the 10-25% highlight band reads warm against the green.

critique.observation: Judged only on states-thumb.png at 120px, with the captions covered I cannot pick out the stress row. It is not that the change is small — it is that the change has no direction. For 138 and 212 the stress frame is CLEANER than neutral: the bars consolidate into two very large unbroken pink blocks and the number of separate rows drops. That is re-locking, which is what the brief asks recovery to do. For 175 the three states are near-identical across all three singles — only the two magenta blocks shift a few pixels and change size. Nothing shears, nothing fragments, no chroma fringe separates.
critique.action: Make stress subtractive and lateral rather than a re-draw: under volatility shear 3-6 contiguous bands (each 8-15% of frame height) sideways by 10-30% of frame width, break each lit row into 2-5 fragments dropping 30-50% of its length, and push the magenta offset from ~1px to 8-12px so the fringe visibly separates from its green row. Under recovery return the offset to 1px, restore row continuity above 95%, and re-align every band to x=0. Then re-render states-thumb and require that the stress column be nameable at 120px with the captions masked.

critique.observation: The round-1 blank-tile failure is fixed — on contact-thumb.png all twelve tiles are visibly non-empty at 120px and none reads as an empty black rectangle. The remaining problem is the second half of the axis. Roughly seven tiles (101, 212, 249, 286, 323, 471, 508) collapse to one stamp: a stack of grey-white bars with a hot-pink slab near the middle. What separates them at browse size is where the pink sits, not what the structure is. 175 fails in the opposite direction — it is a small centred blob carrying maybe a third of the ink of its neighbours and reads as an under-filled tile in the grid.
critique.action: Raise 175's coverage to the same 35-80% lit-row band as the rest of the sheet, then remove hue and pink position as differentiators: vary row pitch per seed across 3-8px, dropout-band count across 0-4 with off-centre placement, shear magnitude, and the solid-row to broken-row ratio. Target: with the sheet desaturated to greyscale, name six seeds from silhouette alone — right now I can name at most three.

critique.observation: Both directions still miss, though less violently than round 1. Too narrow: at full size on contact.png, 101, 212, 249, 323, 471 and 508 are the same construction — a symmetric stack of grey-white bars with one saturated pink rectangle near the vertical centre and a second smaller one below it; swap their hues and I could not sort them. The variation that does exist is carried by the pink slab's height and y-position, which is a colour event, not a structural one. Too wide in one place: 175 carries roughly a third of the ink of its neighbours and 138 and 360 are dominated by wine masses the other ten do not have, so three tiles sit outside the family the other nine define.
critique.action: Move differentiation out of the slab and into the raster: give each seed a distinct row pitch drawn from 3-8px, a dropout-band count from 0-4 at seed-determined y, a shear magnitude from 0-25% of width, and a solid-to-broken row ratio from 0.3-0.9, and hold the pink slab identical in size and position across all twelve. Bring 175 up to the same 35-80% lit-row coverage band and remove the wine mass from 138 and 360 so all twelve draw from one ink budget.

critique.observation: Most frames now run edge to edge horizontally (138, 397, 434, 471, 508, 323), which was the round-1 action and it landed. Two things still work against the brief. 175 in all three singles and all three states is still a centred blob with roughly the outer 25% of the frame black on both sides and about 20% dead at top and bottom. And where hierarchy now exists it is the wrong hierarchy: a single saturated pink rectangle is the focal object in almost every tile, so the frame reads as an object on a screen rather than as a screen with nothing on it.
critique.action: Extend 175's drawing to 100% of the viewBox on all four sides, matching 397. Then move the large-scale event off the pink slab and into the raster: give each frame one or two horizontal dropout BANDS of 8-15% of frame height, placed off-centre, where rows go dark or shear, and let that be the only thing that dominates.

critique.observation: This held in round 1 and some of it has been traded away for the state change. In states.png, 101 neutral, stress and recovery have their pink and wine masses at different heights and different sizes each time, and 212's pink block sits mid-frame in neutral, at the top in stress, and mid-frame again in recovery with a different bar layout around it — that reads as three draws of the same generator rather than one object being deformed. 175 and 434 do hold, and hue assignment is stable everywhere, so the family is never in doubt; the specific token is.
critique.action: Freeze the seed-determined row y-positions and per-row hue assignment across all three states and let stress change only continuity, x-offset and band shear. Concretely, no bar in the stress frame may move more than 2px in y from its neutral position, and no bar may change hue between states.

critique.observation: Located: (1) the regular lattice of small dark-green squares on the extreme margins is still present and is the round-1 finding unaddressed — a 4-across grid across the whole border of 175 in all three states and all three singles, corner specks in 101, 471 and 508, and in 434 a full row of them along the top edge and another along the bottom with several cut in half by the frame; on a black ground they read as registration marks, not dropout. (2) In 101, 249 and 508 there are runs of tiny circles and diamonds sitting inside the pink slab that read as a dotted-stroke bug at 512 and as speckle at 120px. (3) Mixed bleed: in 138 and 397 some green lines run off the left edge while neighbouring bars stop 20-40px short at inconsistent x, so the cuts read as accidental. (4) 508 neutral has one isolated white bar pinned to the extreme bottom edge, detached from the stack. The round-1 centre-mush finding is genuinely gone.
critique.action: Delete the margin square population entirely — it was named last round and it is still on the sheet. Remove the circle/diamond glyph run from the slab fill. Then make bleed a rule rather than a coincidence: every bar either spans the full viewBox width or terminates at a quantised x on a per-seed grid of about 16px, and drop the isolated bottom-edge bar in 508 by requiring every bar to sit within 6px of another lit row.

critique.observation: This axis is now the strongest. Every one of the twelve tiles on contact.png is built from the same vocabulary — full-width horizontal bars, grey-to-white value steps, thin bright green rules, filled slabs — and the round-1 split into a dense family, a blank family and one orthogonal outlier is gone. 397's motif no longer stands apart, and 138, 360 and 471 are now members rather than holes.
critique.action: Preserve this when the pitch and palette work lands: apply the new row-pitch quantisation and the 5% magenta cap to all twelve seeds in one pass rather than per-seed, so no seed acquires an exemption and the single shared vocabulary survives the rebuild.

critique.observation: The brief asks for dense scan-lines and the ghost of a raster, and what is on the sheet is a stripe painting. Counting bars on contact.png I get roughly 20-35 per tile — 175 has about 20 bright bars across 255px of its 512 frame, 323 about 30. Their heights are not on any grid: in the seed-175 single they run 5-12px with gaps of 3-15px, and in 138 the two hot-pink rectangles are each about a third of the tile's height as a single unbroken fill, with 286 built from three such blocks and almost nothing between them. Because nothing repeats at a fixed interval, no raster is implied — I read datamosh, a JPEG smeared sideways, a hot-pink glitch stripe. I did not read a screen carrying no picture. The one element in the whole packet that behaves like a scan-line is the population of faint dark-green full-width threads in 175's margins, and they are so close to the ground value they read as nothing.
critique.action: Build a base raster layer before anything else is drawn: full-viewBox-width rows at a fixed per-seed pitch of 3-6px at 512 (85-170 rows), bar height 1-3px, covering all four edges, and raise those rows off near-black to alpha 0.25-0.35 so they are visible — that is the population currently wasted as 175's invisible dark-green threads. Then cap every drawn bar at 4px height and rebuild every large mass by GROUPING adjacent rows on that same pitch: 138's two 100px-tall pink blocks become about 25 lit rows each, 286's three blocks likewise. No filled rectangle taller than 8px may survive anywhere in the twelve.

critique.observation: Two of the brief's three named roles are inverted and a fourth colour the brief never names is a major mass. On contact.png a saturated hot-pink slab is the largest and brightest object in 11 of 12 tiles and it is what my eye lands on first at every size; in 286 the frame is essentially pink (a magenta block, a maroon block, a second pink block) with green surviving only as a few hairlines. Sampling lit pixels to put a number on what I saw: magenta runs 18-60% of lit area in nine of twelve seeds (286 at 60%, 249 at 48%, 138 at 48%) against a brief that says THIN chroma error. A dark wine/maroon that appears nowhere in the brief is 7-33% of lit area in all twelve — 360 at 33%, 101 at 26%, 138 at 21%. Phosphor green is the majority hue in zero of twelve, and is effectively absent from 101, 360 and 471 (6-8%). The whites read cool grey, not warm. The near-black ground is the one part that is right; it sits back and never competes.
critique.action: Delete the standalone filled magenta rectangle from the reachable space and replace it with a true chroma error: a 1-3px magenta copy of an already-lit green row, offset horizontally, drawn on no more than 5% of lit pixels per frame. Delete the wine/maroon fill entirely — it is a fourth colour and it was named for removal last round. Raise phosphor green to 60-80% of lit area in every one of the twelve, hold warm white at 10-25%, and shift the white from its current cool grey toward roughly #F2EDE0 so the highlight reads warm against the green.

critique.observation: On states-thumb.png with the captions cropped off I could not pick the stress row in any of the twelve columns, and when I enlarged 249, 397 and 471 the change turned out to point the wrong way. In 249 the middle frame CONSOLIDATES — the separate maroon and pink rows merge into one taller mass and the row count drops — which is re-locking, the thing recovery is supposed to do. In 397 the three frames differ only by a few bar lengths. In 471 the middle and bottom frames resemble each other far more than either resembles the top, so neutral is the odd frame out and stress and recovery are near-duplicates. In the seed-175 singles at 512 the stress frame is a tighter, greyer, LESS green version of neutral, the magenta slab sits in the same place at the same size, and recovery is stress with a few background threads removed rather than a return to neutral. Nothing shears, nothing fragments, no chroma fringe separates.
critique.action: Make stress subtractive and lateral rather than a redraw. Under volatility shear 3-6 contiguous bands of 8-15% of frame height sideways by 10-30% of frame width, break every lit row into 2-5 fragments dropping 30-50% of its length, and push the magenta offset from 1px to 8-12px so the fringe visibly separates from its green row. Under recovery return the offset to 1px, restore row continuity above 95%, and re-align every band to x=0 so recovery lands on neutral and not on stress. Then re-render states-thumb, mask the captions, and require the stress column to be nameable in at least 10 of 12 seeds before shipping.

critique.observation: Most frames now run edge to edge horizontally — 323, 397, 508 and 138 use the full width and that is a real gain — but two failures remain. 175 in all three singles and all three states is still a centred blob: the bright stack occupies roughly x=60-430 and y=120-375 of 512, leaving about 25% of the frame dead black on each side and about 20% dead at top and bottom, and it carries visibly less ink than any neighbour on the sheet. 286 is three floating rectangles with large empty black between them. And where hierarchy exists it is the wrong hierarchy: in 11 of 12 tiles the dominant object is a single saturated pink rectangle, so each frame reads as an object placed on a screen rather than as a screen with nothing on it — the brief's 'density is the subject' cannot be true while the subject is a slab.
critique.action: Extend 175's and 286's drawing to 100% of the viewBox on all four sides, matching 323, and bring 175 up to the same lit-row coverage band as the rest of the sheet (it currently sits near 18% against 397's 70%). Then move the largest event off the pink slab and into the raster: give each frame one or two horizontal dropout bands of 8-15% of frame height, placed off-centre, where rows go dark or shear, and let that band be the only thing in the frame that dominates.

critique.observation: The variation that exists is a colour event wearing structural clothes. At full size on contact.png, 101, 212, 249, 434 and 471 are the same construction — a symmetric stack of grey-white bars with one saturated pink rectangle near the vertical centre and a maroon mass beside it — and what separates them is where the pink sits and how tall it is, not what the raster does. In the other direction the spread that does exist is coverage rather than design: 175 carries about a quarter of the ink of 397, and 286 is three blocks on mostly empty black, so those two read as under-rendered members rather than as different works. Row pitch, dropout-band count and shear are not varying at all, because they do not exist yet.
critique.action: Hold the pink element identical in size and vertical position across all twelve, then differentiate on the raster: draw a per-seed row pitch from 3-8px, a dropout-band count from 0-4 at seed-determined y, a shear magnitude from 0-25% of width, and a solid-to-broken row ratio from 0.3-0.9. Constrain every seed to a 35-80% lit-row coverage band so 175 and 286 stop reading as under-inked. Test by desaturating contact.png to greyscale and requiring that six of the twelve be nameable from silhouette alone.

critique.observation: The round-1 blank-tile failure stays fixed: on contact-thumb.png all twelve are visibly non-empty at 120px. From silhouette I can now name six — 138 by its two pink blocks pinned to the top, 286 by its three separated blocks on mostly black, 175 by being the small pale under-inked tile, 323 by being the dark-green dense one with almost no pink, 397 by pink at top and bottom with green throughout, 508 by dense white with pink low. The other six (101, 212, 249, 360, 434, 471) collapse to the same stamp: a stack of grey-white bars with a hot-pink slab near the middle. And in all twelve the first thing readable at 120px is the pink, not the raster — the sheet reads as a pink-slab collection rather than as a broadcast-interference collection.
critique.action: Remove hue and pink-slab position as the differentiators — with magenta held to 5% and the slab frozen, the six-tile collapse becomes a raster problem you can solve with the pitch, dropout-count, shear and broken-row-ratio ranges above. Raise 175 from its current ~18% coverage into the 35-80% band so it stops reading as the under-filled cell in the grid. Re-render contact-thumb at 120px and require twelve nameable silhouettes with the sheet desaturated.

critique.observation: The two findings I raised twice are genuinely gone: the lattice of small dark-green squares on the margins of 175, 434, 471 and 508 is absent from every frame in this packet, and the run of tiny circles and diamonds inside the pink slabs of 101, 249 and 508 is gone too. What remains is smaller. (1) In 286 a single thin green bar is pinned to the extreme bottom edge, roughly 200px below the nearest other mark, and reads as a stray rather than as dropout. (2) Bleed is inconsistent within a frame: in 397, 471 and 101 some bars run off the left edge at x=0 while neighbouring bars stop 20-40px short at arbitrary x, so the short cuts read as accidental rather than as chosen. (3) In 138 the maroon block at the bottom is cut by the frame edge while the composition above it floats clear of that edge, so the cut reads as a crop error. (4) In the seed-175 singles the pale overlapping bars immediately under the magenta slab stack into a light-grey band about 120px wide where individual bar edges stop being separable — milder than round 1's mush but still present in all three states.
critique.action: Require every bar to either span the full viewBox width or terminate at a quantised x on a per-seed 16px grid, which converts 397's and 471's ragged cuts into a decision. Drop 286's orphan by requiring every bar to sit within 6px of another lit row. Bleed 138's bottom maroon mass deliberately by extending its rows past the viewBox on both sides. For the 175 grey band, give the overlapping pale bars a 1px darker outline or drop their fill opacity to about 0.4 so edges stay separable when three or more stack.

critique.observation: This is the strongest axis and it holds without qualification. Every one of the twelve tiles on contact.png is built from one visible vocabulary — full-bleed horizontal bars, value-stepped overlaps where bars cross, thin bright green rules, semi-transparent slabs that tint what they sit on. The round-1 split into a dense family, a blank family and one orthogonal outlier is entirely gone: 397 no longer stands apart, and 138, 360 and 471 are members. Even the two weak tiles (175, 286) are recognisably from the same generator, they are just under-rendered. Nothing on the sheet looks borrowed from a different project.
critique.action: Apply the row-pitch quantisation, the 5% magenta cap and the wine deletion to all twelve seeds in one pass rather than per-seed, so no seed acquires an exemption and this single shared vocabulary survives the rebuild intact.

critique.observation: This recovered from round 2. Reading states.png row by row, 138 keeps both pink slabs at the same height and size across neutral, stress and recovery and keeps its maroon block at the bottom in all three; 212 keeps its pink block at the top and its second pink block at the bottom in all three, where last round it migrated to the top under stress. In the enlarged states-thumb columns, 249's pink slab stays at the top in all three states and 471's pink stays mid-frame in all three. Hue assignment per bar is stable everywhere. 101 still moves its mauve and maroon masses a few pixels in y between states, but the token is never in doubt. Recovery lands close to neutral in form even where it does not land close in state.
critique.action: Freeze this before adding the shear and fragmentation the market-response axis needs: hold the seed-determined row y-positions and per-row hue assignment identical across all three states, allow stress to change only continuity, x-offset and band shear, and enforce that no bar moves more than 2px in y or changes hue between neutral and stress — including 101's mauve mass, which is the one that still drifts.

critique.observation: The brief asks for a monumental upright slab. What is on the sheet is a small chip. In singles--seed175-neutral.png the form is roughly 55x85px inside a 512px frame -- about 11% of the width and 17% of the height -- sitting in the dead centre of an otherwise empty field. The largest seeds on contact.png (138, 508, 397) reach only about a third of the cell height. Sparsity is delivered; monumentality is not. Nothing in any of the twelve frames establishes scale, so the object reads as a specimen tile mounted on a card rather than a slab you stand under. 'Upright' also fails outright on several seeds: 138 is nearly square, and 249 and 508 are wider than they are tall, i.e. lying down.
critique.action: Raise the neutral form to roughly 55-70% of frame HEIGHT (a 3-4x linear increase on the current median) and let it break or nearly touch the bottom edge so it stands on the ground rather than hovering. Clamp the aspect ratio so height/width is never below about 1.4:1 -- reject the landscape draws entirely rather than letting the seed produce them.

critique.observation: Every one of the 36 frames on states.png places the form at the same centred-left position with an even margin of void on all four sides. The frame is never used -- there is no base, no horizon, no crop, no edge contact anywhere in the packet. With only one object there is a focal subject by default, but it commands nothing, because it is small and equidistant from every boundary. The negative space is empty rather than charged.
critique.action: Anchor the form to the lower third: put its base at roughly 82-88% of frame height and let the void sit above it, so the emptiness reads as sky over a standing object rather than as uniform padding. Vary horizontal placement by seed across about the middle 40% of the frame instead of pinning every seed to one x.

critique.observation: This is the most serious failure and it is visible in every stress cell of states.png. Under drawdown the slab does not crack -- it is deleted and replaced. Seed 138 goes from a tall pale portrait slab with a dark bar near its top to a mid-grey LANDSCAPE block with a T-shaped notch, plus a second detached dark block floating below and to the left. Seed 175 goes from one upright cream rectangle to two thin horizontal cream bars plus an unrelated olive-grey block 80px lower. Aspect flips portrait to landscape, one body becomes two, the position moves, and the fill tone changes. Nothing carries across. That is a different object, not a damaged one.
critique.action: Preserve the neutral silhouette's bounding box, aspect ratio and centroid exactly through all three states, and express stress ONLY as subtractive fracture inside it: 2-4 fissure lines of ground colour cutting the slab, with the resulting fragments offset by no more than about 3-5% of the slab's width. No new bodies, no re-proportioning, no relocation. The viewer should be able to lay neutral over stress and see the same outline.

critique.observation: The stress row on states-thumb.png is genuinely distinguishable from the neutral row -- one blob becomes two stacked blobs with a gap -- so the transition is not invisible, which is the one thing this axis most often fails on. But it is not the change the brief claims. 'Crack' reads as a split-and-scatter. In the other direction, recovery is nearly undeliverable at browse size: on the 120px sheet, seeds 212, 249, 286, 360, 397, 471 and 508 have recovery frames I cannot tell apart from their neutral frames. Only 101 (a bold diagonal band) and to a lesser degree 138 and 175 show a healed scar. The full-size singles--seed175-recovery.png has two hairline diagonals about 1px wide -- they are gone by 120px.
critique.action: Two changes. (1) Re-cut stress as fracture inside the silhouette, per the tokenIdentity note. (2) Make the recovery scar carry to thumbnail: raise scar stroke width to about 2.5-3% of the slab's short dimension (roughly 4-6x the current hairline) and give it a fixed value offset from the slab fill of at least 25% luminance, so the healed seam is the thing that distinguishes recovery from neutral at 120px rather than a detail that only exists at 512.

critique.observation: On contact-thumb.png, seeds 286, 471, 212, 434 and 360 are dark grey rectangles on a near-black ground with so little separation that they read as smudges; 286 in particular is close to invisible. The single piece of internal structure the design carries -- the horizontal band split -- vanishes on roughly half the seeds at 120px, so those tokens collapse to 'small grey rectangle' and become interchangeable. Across the whole neutral row I can distinguish about five classes, not twelve. On states-thumb.png the neutral and recovery rows are close to the same row.
critique.action: Impose a hard minimum contrast floor between slab fill and ground -- no seed's fill below roughly 45% luminance against a ~7% ground -- and cut the low end of the value ramp entirely rather than compressing it. Raise the internal band divider to at least 2% of slab height so it survives downsampling. Then re-render the 120px sheet and require that all twelve neutrals are individually nameable before anything else is tuned.

critique.observation: The brief says two tones: a dark ground and one pale stone. Individual frames sometimes honour that -- seed 175 neutral is genuinely cream on near-black. The collection does not. contact.png shows a continuous grey ramp from a charcoal barely above the ground (212, 286, 471) up to full cream (175), which is a value jitter rather than a chosen pair. Worse, stress puts three tones in a single frame: singles--seed175-stress.png has pale cream bars, a distinctly mid olive-grey block below them, and the near-black ground. That third body's tone belongs to neither declared tone.
critique.action: Fix ONE pale stone value for the whole collection and let seeds vary geometry instead of fill. If a value axis is wanted, cap it at about two steps (say 100% and 80% of the stone value) rather than a continuous ramp, and never let a fill land within 30% luminance of the ground. Any fragment produced by stress must be drawn in the same single stone value as the slab it came from.

critique.observation: Laid out on contact.png the twelve seeds vary along exactly three parameters: overall scale, fill lightness, and how many horizontal bands are drawn (one, two, or three). Every form is an axis-aligned rectangle with horizontal-only subdivision, centred. It is recognisably one work at twelve settings rather than twelve works. The opposite failure is not present -- there is no risk of this stopping being one project.
critique.action: Add one or two structural axes that stay inside the two-tone, few-marks constraint: vary the slab's proportion meaningfully (from about 1.4:1 to 4:1 tall-and-narrow), and let the internal division be positional rather than count-based -- a single seam whose height along the slab moves through the seed range, occasionally a vertical seam. Keep total marks per token at 1-3. Do not add colour or ornament to buy variation.

critique.observation: This axis is the work's real strength. Every frame on contact.png is unmistakably from the same hand -- same reductive vocabulary, same ground, same restraint, same silence. Nothing looks imported from another project. Whatever is changed in revision, this discipline is what should be protected.
critique.action: No change required. When raising scale and contrast per the notes above, hold the vocabulary fixed -- resist adding textures, gradients or a third element to compensate for the added emptiness.

critique.observation: No clipping at the frame edge and nothing cut by the viewBox anywhere in the packet. But several shapes carry notches that read as boolean-subtraction accidents rather than marks: on states.png, 101 stress has a stepped bite cut out of the upper block's lower-left corner; 212 stress has a rectangular bite out of the upper block's right side and a stray pale triangular sliver inside the lower block; 434 stress (visible on states-thumb.png) has a dark triangular wedge cutting the lower block's left edge. 138 stress shows a lighter T-shaped region inside the upper block that reads as two rectangles of different fill overlapping with the wrong z-order. On contact.png, 212 neutral has a small pale tab overhanging the slab's top-right corner that looks like a mis-registered second rect rather than a feature.
critique.action: Snap every fragment edge to the parent slab's own edges so subtraction can only produce clean rectilinear cuts, and forbid any fragment from extending outside the parent bounding box (that kills the 212 neutral tab). Resolve overlapping fills by unioning same-tone shapes before render rather than stacking them, which removes the 138 T-shape.

critique.observation: The brief's first sentence is 'One slab... and nothing else in the frame.' There is no slab anywhere in this packet, and there is never only one thing. Every one of the twelve neutral cells on contact.png is TWO detached rectangles stacked with a void between them: 101 is a small pale chip over a mid-grey bar, 175 is a cream block over an olive-grey block separated by roughly 80px of ground, 508 is a dark block over a pale block. That pattern holds 12 out of 12, and it holds through all 36 cells of states-thumb.png. Worse for the noun, all 24 rectangles on contact.png are wider than tall or square -- 138's upper block is about 122x88, 397's about 126x92, 249's about 128x58, 360's lower block about 46x44. Not one upright form exists in the packet. Monumentality is also absent: the tallest single body (397 upper) fills about a third of its 277px cell height and nothing touches or approaches the bottom edge, so every token still reads as specimen chips floating on a card. Round 1 asked for an aspect clamp of height/width >= 1.4:1 and the landscape draws rejected; what shipped is the inverse, plus a second body.
critique.action: Delete the second rectangle entirely -- render exactly ONE body per token -- and clamp the surviving slab to height/width >= 1.6:1, rejecting any seed draw below that rather than squashing it. Scale that slab to 60-70% of frame height (about 3x the current median linear size) and put its base at 85% of frame height so it stands on the ground instead of hovering.

critique.observation: With two bodies of near-equal mass in every frame there is now no focal subject at all. In 323, 434, 471 and 360 the lower block is the larger or the lighter of the pair, so the eye is pulled downward; in 138 and 508 the upper block dominates; in 397 and 212 the two are close enough that neither wins. The result is an even field of two incidents, which is the specific failure the rubric names. The frame is still never used: across all 36 cells of states.png and states-thumb.png nothing touches the bottom edge, nothing is cropped, there is no base or horizon, and the void is a uniform margin on all four sides rather than charged space. The one near-edge event -- 138's upper block starting about 13px from the cell top -- reads as an accident of scale, not as a crop.
critique.action: After collapsing to one body, anchor its base at 84-88% of frame height so the void becomes sky above a standing object, and let the slab's top exit the top edge on roughly 1 seed in 4 so the frame crops the monument instead of containing it. Scatter horizontal placement across the middle 40% of the frame by seed rather than pinning every seed to centre.

critique.observation: This remains the work's one intact strength. Laid out on contact.png the twelve frames are unmistakably from one hand: same near-black ground, same matte flat fills with no stroke, no gradient, no texture, no ornament, same silence. Nothing looks imported from another project, and the round-1 warning about compensating for emptiness with added incident was heeded -- no textures or third elements have been bolted on.
critique.action: Hold this vocabulary fixed while executing the scale and single-body changes above: keep the axis-aligned rectangle, the flat unstroked fill and the matte near-black ground exactly as they are, and buy the new variation from proportion and seam position rather than from any new mark type.

critique.observation: The brief says two tones. Every frame in the packet now carries three. singles--seed175-neutral.png has a cream upper block, a distinctly mid olive-grey lower block and the near-black ground -- the mid-grey belongs to neither declared tone, and the same three-tone structure repeats across all twelve seeds on contact.png with the two fills differing within nearly every frame (249 dark-over-pale, 286 dark-over-pale, 323 mid-over-pale, 138 pale-over-charcoal). On top of that the fill ramp is still continuous rather than chosen: 212 and 434 sit barely above the ground in both blocks while 175 is full cream. This is the round-1 finding unchanged, and the second body has made it structural instead of incidental.
critique.action: Fix ONE pale stone value for the whole collection and let seeds vary geometry only; deleting the second body removes the second fill for free. Enforce a hard floor of at least 30% luminance separation between any fill and the ground so the 212 and 434 charcoals are cut out of the ramp entirely rather than compressed toward it, and draw any stress fragment in exactly the same stone value as the slab it came from.

critique.observation: Across contact.png the twelve seeds still vary on only three parameters: overall scale, fill lightness, and the size of the gap between the two blocks. Every one of the 24 shapes is an axis-aligned rectangle, every one is landscape, every one is horizontally centred. The block-pair arrangement adds a little more signature than round 1's single band-split (138's big-pale-over-dark is genuinely a different silhouette from 471's two tiny chips), but this is still one work at twelve settings. The opposite failure is absent -- nothing here threatens to stop being one project.
critique.action: Once there is a single body, drive its proportion across a real range by seed -- about 1.6:1 through 4.5:1 tall-and-narrow -- and make the internal division positional rather than count-based: one seam whose height travels from 15% to 85% up the slab through the seed range, vertical on roughly 2 seeds in 12. Cap total marks per token at 2 and add no colour or ornament to buy the difference.

critique.observation: On contact-thumb.png at 120px I can name about eight of the twelve by their block-pair signature -- 138 (large pale over dark), 397 (two large warm greys), 175 (bright cream chip over grey bar), 249 (dark over large pale), 508 (large dark over pale), 286 (small dark over pale bar), 323 (mid over pale), 360 (dark bar over tiny pale chip).
